# General relativity {#sec-general-relativity}

General relativity is the theory of gravitation in which the metric of spacetime is itself the dynamical field:
matter tells spacetime how to curve, through the Einstein equations, and spacetime tells matter how to move, along
its geodesics. Newton's law of gravitation is recovered for weak fields and slow motion, and the corrections to it
are the classic tests of the theory: the advance of the perihelion of Mercury, the bending of light by the Sun and
the gravitational redshift. This chapter has three sections. The Einstein-Hilbert action introduces spacetime and the
equivalence principle, shows how the geodesic equation reproduces Newton's law, and defines the action of the
gravitational field together with the formulas needed to vary it. The Einstein equations carries out the variation,
defines the stress tensor and the cosmological constant, and studies the maximally symmetric vacuum solutions, de
Sitter and anti-de Sitter space. Black holes and cosmology solves the equations in the two settings where they are
used most: the Schwarzschild solution outside a spherical mass, with its horizon and its orbits, and the expanding
homogeneous universe of Friedmann, Lemaître, Robertson and Walker. We use the signature $(+, -, -, -)$ of
@sec-conventions-indices throughout, in which the scalar curvature of a sphere-like (de Sitter) spacetime is negative
and the action carries an overall minus sign. Minkowski spacetime, the flat spacetime of special relativity on which every spacetime is modelled
locally, and the Rindler frame of uniformly accelerated observers, whose clocks behave as clocks in a gravitational field,
are developed in @sec-special-relativity (@sec-sr-minkowski, @sec-sr-dynamics). Every statement is followed by three examples and three exercises with
hidden solutions.

## The Einstein-Hilbert action {#sec-einstein-hilbert}

Kaluza-Klein theory is general relativity in more than four dimensions, so its input is the action of general
relativity, and Part III consists of evaluating that action on a five-dimensional metric. This section defines
spacetime, states the equivalence principle, shows how the geodesic equation of Part I reproduces Newton's law,
and introduces the Einstein-Hilbert action together with the two variational formulas its variation needs. Our
source is @carroll1997, who uses the signature $(-, +, +, +)$; we convert to our $(+, -, -, -)$ with the rule of
@sec-conventions-indices, which flips the signs of $R$ and of the gravitational Lagrangian but not those of
$\Gamma$, $R^\rho{}_{\sigma\mu\nu}$ and $R_{\mu\nu}$, and we note his different normalisation of the action where it
matters.

### Spacetime and the equivalence principle

The arena of general relativity is a manifold with a metric, exactly as in the geometry of @sec-metrics, except that
the metric is not positive definite. The sign of $g(v, v)$ then sorts tangent vectors, and curves, into three
classes with different physical meanings.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-spacetime}
#### Spacetime

A **spacetime** is a four-dimensional manifold (@def-manifold) with a metric $g_{\mu\nu}$ of Lorentzian signature
$(+, -, -, -)$ (@def-signature-metric). Curves with $g_{\mu\nu}\dot x^\mu\dot x^\nu > 0$ are **timelike**, the possible
worldlines of massive particles; those with $g_{\mu\nu}\dot x^\mu\dot x^\nu = 0$ are **null**, the worldlines of
light; the remaining ones are **spacelike**.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first example is the spacetime of special relativity, flat and with the largest possible symmetry group. Every
other spacetime looks like it in a small enough neighbourhood of any point, which is the content of the equivalence
principle below.

::: {#exm-spacetime-minkowski}
#### Minkowski spacetime

$\mathbb{R}^4$ with $\eta = \operatorname{diag}(1, -1, -1, -1)$ (@exm-metric-minkowski), the spacetime of special
relativity. Its Christoffel symbols vanish (@exm-christoffel-constant), so it is flat, and its isometry group is
the Poincaré group of translations and Lorentz transformations, of dimension $10 = 4 \cdot 5/2$, the maximum
(@def-maximally-symmetric).
:::

The second example is curved and expanding. It reappears throughout the chapter: as a vacuum solution with a
cosmological constant in @sec-einstein-equations and as a cosmological model in @sec-schwarzschild-flrw.

::: {#exm-spacetime-de-sitter}
#### De Sitter space

$ds^2 = dt^2 - e^{2Ht}(dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2)$ with constant $H > 0$ describes an exponentially expanding universe:
**de Sitter space** in flat slicing, the Lorentzian analogue of the sphere, maximally symmetric with positive
curvature, whose curvature is computed in @sec-einstein-equations.
:::

Spacetimes need not be four-dimensional; the definition makes sense in any dimension with one time and several space
directions. Higher-dimensional products are the starting point of the reductions studied in the main theme.

::: {#exm-spacetime-product}
#### Product spacetimes

$M_4 \times S^1$ with $ds^2 = \eta_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu - R^2dy^2$ (@def-product-metric with the sign of the
internal metric reversed), the spacetime of Part III, is a five-dimensional Lorentzian manifold; $M_4 \times S/R$
with minus the invariant metric of @def-invariant-metric on the coset is the spacetime of Part V. Both have the
signature $(+, -, \dots, -)$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The causal character of a vector depends only on the sign of its norm, and this sign is computed with the metric.
The first exercise does this for a few vectors and a family of worldlines in Minkowski space.

::: {#exr-gr-causal-character}
#### Timelike, null and spacelike

Classify the vectors $(1, 0, 0, 0)$, $(1, 1, 0, 0)$, $(1, 2, 0, 0)$ and $(0, 0, 1, 0)$ of Minkowski space, and show
that the worldline $x^\mu(t) = (t, vt, 0, 0)$ is timelike exactly when $|v| < 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $\eta = \operatorname{diag}(1, -1, -1, -1)$ the norms are $1$, $0$, $-3$ and $-1$: timelike, null, spacelike,
spacelike. The tangent of the worldline is $(1, v, 0, 0)$ with norm $1 - v^2$, positive exactly when $|v| < 1$: a
massive particle moves slower than light, and $|v| = 1$ is a light ray.
:::

A metric that looks curved may be flat space in unusual coordinates; only the Riemann tensor decides. The Rindler
metric of a uniformly accelerated observer is the standard example, and the exercise computes its curvature with
SageManifolds.

::: {#exr-gr-rindler}
#### Rindler space

Show that $ds^2 = x^2dt^2 - dx^2 - dy^2 - dz^2$ on $x > 0$ has non-zero Christoffel symbols but vanishing Riemann
tensor, and find the coordinate change to Minkowski space.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The non-zero symbols are $\Gamma^x_{tt} = x$ and $\Gamma^t_{tx} = 1/x$; the Riemann tensor vanishes, so the space is
flat (@def-riemann). Indeed $T = x\sinh t$, $X = x\cosh t$ give $dT^2 - dX^2 = x^2dt^2 - dx^2$: the Rindler wedge
$X > |T|$ of Minkowski space, whose observers at fixed $x$ have constant proper acceleration $1/x$.

{{< sage exr-gr-rindler >}}
:::

The length of a timelike curve is the time shown by a clock carried along it. The third exercise computes it for a
circular worldline, the relativistic version of the twin paradox.

::: {#exr-gr-proper-time}
#### Proper time on a circle

The **proper time** along a timelike curve is $\tau = \int\sqrt{g_{\mu\nu}\dot x^\mu\dot x^\nu}\,dt$. Compute it for
$x^\mu(t) = (t, R\cos\omega t, R\sin\omega t, 0)$, $0 \leq t \leq T$, in Minkowski space, and compare with the
proper time $T$ of an observer at rest.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The tangent is $(1, -R\omega\sin\omega t, R\omega\cos\omega t, 0)$ with norm $1 - R^2\omega^2$, constant and positive
for $R\omega < 1$; hence $\tau = T\sqrt{1 - R^2\omega^2} < T$. The travelling clock is younger: among timelike curves
between two events the straight one, a geodesic, has the largest proper time, the Lorentzian opposite of the
shortest-path property of Riemannian geodesics.
:::
::::

Special relativity knows nothing of gravity, and the step to general relativity is a physical principle rather
than a theorem. Its content is that a gravitational field can be removed locally by free fall, so that gravity
becomes a property of the metric instead of a force.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-equivalence-principle}
#### Equivalence principle

The **equivalence principle** is the statement that in a freely falling frame the laws of physics are locally
those of special relativity: gravity is not a force but the curvature of spacetime, and free particles move on
geodesics (@def-geodesic) of $g_{\mu\nu}$. Mathematically it is the existence, at every point, of coordinates in
which $g_{\mu\nu} = \eta_{\mu\nu}$ and $\partial_\rho g_{\mu\nu} = 0$ (Riemann normal coordinates); the second
derivatives, the curvature of @sec-riemann, cannot be transformed away.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The most familiar illustration is a freely falling laboratory. Inside it gravity disappears at a point, and only its
variation across the laboratory survives.

::: {#exm-equivalence-elevator}
#### The falling elevator

Inside a freely falling box no local experiment detects the gravitational field: objects released at rest stay
at rest relative to the box. Only the relative acceleration of two separated objects, the geodesic deviation
governed by the Riemann tensor (@def-riemann), reveals gravity.
:::

The geodesics of a metric are the candidate trajectories of free particles. Two spaces from earlier in the book
illustrate this, the sphere and de Sitter space.

::: {#exm-equivalence-geodesics}
#### Free fall as geodesic motion

On the sphere, great circles are the geodesics (@exr-sphere-geodesic); in de Sitter space in flat slicing, curves
of constant $(x, y, z)$ are timelike geodesics, the comoving observers, since $\Gamma^i_{tt} = 0$
(@prp-de-sitter). The equivalence principle makes such curves the trajectories of freely falling bodies.
:::

The principle also says how matter feels gravity, by a mechanical replacement rule. This rule is used for every
matter field of the book.

::: {#exm-equivalence-coupling}
#### Minimal coupling

The equivalence principle fixes how matter couples to gravity: take the special-relativistic action of
@sec-actions, replace $\eta_{\mu\nu}$ by $g_{\mu\nu}$, $\partial_\mu$ by $\nabla_\mu$ (@def-covariant-derivative-vector)
and $d^4x$ by $\sqrt{-g}\,d^4x$ (@def-volume-element). For a scalar, $S = \int d^4x\sqrt{-g}\,(\tfrac12g^{\mu\nu}
\partial_\mu\phi\partial_\nu\phi - V)$, the form used throughout Parts III to V.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The equivalence principle fixes the metric and its first derivatives at a point, and the following counting argument
shows that exactly the curvature is left over. It is the standard argument of @carroll1997 [section 2.9].

::: {#exr-gr-normal-coordinates}
#### Counting the curvature

At a point $p$ of a four-dimensional spacetime, count the Taylor coefficients of $g_{\mu\nu}$ of order zero, one and
two, and the coefficients of a coordinate change $x \mapsto x'$ available to set them to their flat values. Show
that $20$ second-order coefficients survive, and compare with the number of independent components of the Riemann
tensor.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$g_{\mu\nu}$ is symmetric: $10$ values at $p$, $10 \cdot 4 = 40$ first derivatives and $10 \cdot 10 = 100$ second
derivatives. A change of coordinates has $16$ first derivatives $\partial x'/\partial x$, $4 \cdot 10 = 40$ second
derivatives and $4 \cdot 20 = 80$ third derivatives. The $16$ are enough to set $g_{\mu\nu}(p) = \eta_{\mu\nu}$ with
$6$ left over, the Lorentz group; the $40$ set $\partial g(p) = 0$ exactly; of the $100$ second derivatives only $80$
can be removed, and $20$ remain. This is the number of independent components of the Riemann tensor in four
dimensions, $n^2(n^2 - 1)/12 = 20$ (@def-riemann-lowered).
:::

The falling elevator of the examples feels the variation of the field across it. In the Newtonian limit this
variation is the second derivative of the potential, and the next exercise computes it for a point mass.

::: {#exr-gr-tidal}
#### Tidal forces

Two freely falling particles at $\vec x$ and $\vec x + \vec\xi$ in a Newtonian potential $\Phi$ have relative
acceleration $\ddot\xi^i = -(\partial_i\partial_j\Phi)\xi^j$ to first order in $\xi$. Compute the tidal matrix
$-\partial_i\partial_j\Phi$ for $\Phi = -GM/r$ at the point $(r, 0, 0)$, and estimate the tidal acceleration across a
body of height $2\,$m at $400\,$km above the Earth.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The matrix is $\tfrac{GM}{r^3}\operatorname{diag}(2, -1, -1)$: stretching along the radius and compression across it,
with zero trace because $\nabla^2\Phi = 0$ in vacuum. In general relativity this matrix is $R^i{}_{tjt}$, the
geodesic deviation of @exm-equivalence-elevator. Over $2\,$m in low Earth orbit the stretching is about
$5 \times 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, imperceptible; near a stellar black hole it tears bodies apart.

{{< sage exr-gr-tidal >}}
:::

Minimal coupling turns a special-relativistic action into a generally covariant one. The last exercise applies the
rule to the electromagnetic field and finds that the field strength needs no Christoffel symbols at all.

::: {#exr-gr-minimal-maxwell}
#### Minimal coupling of the Maxwell field

Apply the rule of @exm-equivalence-coupling to the Maxwell action $-\tfrac14\int d^4x\,F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}$ with
$F_{\mu\nu} = \partial_\mu A_\nu - \partial_\nu A_\mu$. Show that $\nabla_\mu A_\nu - \nabla_\nu A_\mu = \partial_\mu A_\nu -
\partial_\nu A_\mu$ and write the resulting action.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\nabla_\mu A_\nu = \partial_\mu A_\nu - \Gamma^\rho_{\mu\nu}A_\rho$ (@def-covariant-derivative-tensor), and the
Christoffel term is symmetric in $\mu\nu$ (@def-torsion: the Levi-Civita connection is torsion free), so it cancels in
the antisymmetric combination. The covariant action is $S = -\tfrac14\int d^4x\sqrt{-g}\,g^{\mu\rho}g^{\nu\sigma}
F_{\mu\nu}F_{\rho\sigma}$: the metric enters only through the contractions and the volume element, which is where the
stress tensor of @exm-stress-maxwell comes from.
:::

The equivalence principle says that inertial forces are gravitational fields of a kind. The next exercise makes this
concrete for a rotating frame in flat spacetime, where the Christoffel symbols turn out to be the centrifugal and
Coriolis forces.

::: {#exr-grb-rotating-frame}
#### Centrifugal and Coriolis forces as Christoffel symbols

In Minkowski space with cylindrical coordinates, pass to a frame rotating with angular velocity $\omega$ about the $z$-axis,
$\phi = \phi' + \omega t$. Write the metric in $(t, r, \phi', z)$, compute its non-zero Christoffel symbols, and show that in the
non-relativistic limit $d\tau \approx dt$ the geodesic equations become $\ddot r - r\dot\phi'^2 = \omega^2r + 2\omega r\dot\phi'$ and
$r\ddot\phi' + 2\dot r\dot\phi' = -2\omega\dot r$. Identify the forces. Where does $g_{tt}$ vanish? [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 2.115]
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$ds^2 = (1 - \omega^2r^2)dt^2 - 2\omega r^2\,dt\,d\phi' - dr^2 - r^2d\phi'^2 - dz^2$. The non-zero symbols are $\Gamma^r_{tt} = -\omega^2r$,
$\Gamma^r_{t\phi'} = -\omega r$, $\Gamma^r_{\phi'\phi'} = -r$, $\Gamma^{\phi'}_{tr} = \omega/r$ and $\Gamma^{\phi'}_{r\phi'} = 1/r$ (with their symmetric
partners). The geodesic equations $\ddot x^\mu = -\Gamma^\mu_{\nu\rho}\dot x^\nu\dot x^\rho$ with $\dot t = 1$ give $\ddot r = \omega^2r + 2\omega r\dot\phi' + r\dot\phi'^2$
and $\ddot\phi' = -2(\omega + \dot\phi')\dot r/r$, the stated equations; they are the free motion $\ddot r = r\dot\phi^2$, $(r^2\dot\phi)^\cdot = 0$ of
the inertial frame rewritten with $\dot\phi = \dot\phi' + \omega$. The term $\omega^2r$ is the centrifugal acceleration and $2\omega r\dot\phi'$,
$-2\omega\dot r/r$ are the components of the Coriolis acceleration $-2\vec\omega\times\vec v$. $g_{tt} = 0$ at $\omega r = 1$: beyond this
"light cylinder" a point at rest in the rotating frame would move faster than light, and no observer can be at rest there.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

### The Newtonian limit

Newton's theory works extremely well in the solar system, so general relativity must reduce to it when fields are
weak and velocities small. The following definition makes this regime precise and identifies the Newtonian potential
inside the metric.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-newtonian-limit}
#### Newtonian limit

The **Newtonian limit** of a metric is the regime of a weak static field, $g_{\mu\nu} = \eta_{\mu\nu} + h_{\mu\nu}$
with $|h| \ll 1$ and $\partial_th = 0$, and slowly moving particles, $|\dot x^i| \ll 1$. In it the geodesic equation
@eq-geodesic reduces to $\ddot x^i = -\Gamma^i_{tt}$, and with $h_{tt} = 2\Phi$ the Christoffel symbol is
$\Gamma^i_{tt} = \tfrac12 g^{ii}(-\partial_i g_{tt}) = \partial_i\Phi$ to first order, so $\ddot x^i = -\partial_i\Phi$:
Newton's law with $\Phi$ the gravitational potential [@carroll1997, eqs. 4.19-4.21, where $h_{tt} = -2\Phi$ in his
signature] (@prp-newtonian-limit, @fig-newtonian-limit).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first example is the field of a point mass. It anticipates the exact solution of @sec-schwarzschild-flrw, whose
time component it reproduces at large distance.

::: {#exm-newtonian-point-mass}
#### A point mass

$\Phi = -GM/r$ gives $g_{tt} = 1 - 2GM/r$: the first term of the Schwarzschild metric, and the orbits of the
weak-field geodesics are Kepler's ellipses up to a slow precession of the perihelion, the first post-Newtonian
correction (@fig-newtonian-limit).
:::

The metric component $g_{tt}$ also governs the rate of clocks. This gives the first effect of gravity on time,
measured to high precision on the Earth and essential for satellite navigation.

::: {#exm-newtonian-redshift}
#### Gravitational redshift

A clock at rest measures proper time $d\tau = \sqrt{g_{tt}}\,dt = (1 + \Phi)dt$: clocks deeper in the potential
run slower, and light climbing out of a potential well is redshifted by $\Delta\nu/\nu = -\Delta\Phi$, the first
confirmed consequence of the equivalence principle.
:::

Weak-field limits also organise the extra fields of higher-dimensional theories. The scalar of the five-dimensional
theory is the simplest case.

::: {#exm-newtonian-kk}
#### The Kaluza-Klein scalar as a Newtonian field

In Part III the fifth-dimension component $g_{55} = \phi^2$ enters the four-dimensional action as a scalar field;
its weak-field limit is a Brans-Dicke-type correction to Newton's law, which is why the radius of the fifth
dimension must be stabilised.
:::

The redshift of @exm-newtonian-redshift was first measured in a laboratory, over the height of a building. The next
example puts in the numbers of that experiment, which show how small the effect is near the Earth.

::: {#exm-grb-pound-rebka}
#### The Pound-Rebka experiment

Near the surface of the Earth $\Phi = gz$ up to a constant, so light sent down a tower of height $h$ arrives blueshifted by
$\Delta\nu/\nu = gh/c^2$. For $h = 22.5\,$m, $\Delta\nu/\nu = 9.81 \times 22.5/(3.00 \times 10^8)^2 = 2.45 \times 10^{-15}$, the shift measured by
Pound and Rebka in 1960 with the Mössbauer effect. By the equivalence principle the same shift is the Doppler shift seen in a
frame accelerating upwards with $g$: during the travel time $h/c$ the receiver gains the speed $gh/c$ towards the
source [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 2.113].
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
How weak is the gravitational field of familiar bodies? The dimensionless number $\Phi/c^2$ at the surface answers
this, and the first exercise compares it for four kinds of objects.

::: {#exr-gr-surface-potential}
#### How weak is weak

Evaluate $|\Phi|/c^2 = GM/(Rc^2)$ at the surface of the Earth ($GM = 3.99 \times 10^{14}\,\mathrm{m^3/s^2}$, $R = 6371\,$km),
the Sun ($GM = 1.33 \times 10^{20}\,\mathrm{m^3/s^2}$, $R = 6.96 \times 10^5\,$km), a white dwarf ($0.6$ solar masses,
$R = 7000\,$km) and a neutron star ($1.4$ solar masses, $R = 12\,$km). Where does the Newtonian limit fail?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $c^2 = 8.99 \times 10^{16}\,\mathrm{m^2/s^2}$: Earth $7 \times 10^{-10}$, Sun $2.1 \times 10^{-6}$, white dwarf
$1.3 \times 10^{-4}$, neutron star $0.17$. The first three are deep in the Newtonian regime, with relativistic
corrections of the order of these numbers; for a neutron star the corrections are of order one, and its structure
needs the full Einstein equations.
:::

Clocks on navigation satellites are higher in the potential and move faster than clocks on the ground, and the two
effects have opposite signs. The second exercise computes both for the GPS orbit.

::: {#exr-gr-gps-clock}
#### The GPS clocks

A clock in the weak field moving with speed $v$ runs at $d\tau = (1 + \Phi/c^2 - v^2/2c^2)\,dt$ to first order.
Compare a GPS satellite on a circular orbit of radius $26\,561\,$km with a clock on the surface of the Earth (ignore
the Earth's rotation), over one day.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The higher potential makes the satellite clock gain $GM(1/R_E - 1/r)/c^2 \times 1\,\text{day} = 45.7\,\mu$s; its
orbital speed, $v^2 = GM/r$, makes it lose $7.2\,\mu$s. The net gain of $38.5\,\mu$s per day would, uncorrected,
shift positions by about $11\,$km per day, so the satellite clocks are deliberately detuned before launch.

{{< sage exr-gr-gps-clock >}}
:::

Newton's law is not the only thing the weak-field geodesic equation knows; the time component gives the conservation
of energy. The third exercise derives the Newtonian energy from the conserved quantity of a static metric.

::: {#exr-gr-nl-energy}
#### Energy conservation in the Newtonian limit

For a static metric, $E = g_{tt}\,dt/d\tau$ is constant along geodesics (it is the conserved quantity of the Killing
vector $\partial_t$, @def-killing). Show that for $g_{tt} = 1 + 2\Phi$, $g_{ij} = -(1 - 2\Phi)\delta_{ij}$ and a slow
particle, $E = 1 + \tfrac12v^2 + \Phi$ to first order in $\Phi$ and $v^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
From $d\tau^2 = (1 + 2\Phi)dt^2 - (1 - 2\Phi)d\vec x^2$, $dt/d\tau = (1 + 2\Phi - (1 - 2\Phi)v^2)^{-1/2} \approx 1 - \Phi +
\tfrac12v^2$. Then $E = (1 + 2\Phi)(1 - \Phi + \tfrac12v^2) \approx 1 + \Phi + \tfrac12v^2$: the rest energy plus the
Newtonian energy per unit mass, which is therefore conserved.
:::
::::

The Newtonian limit has two sides: the connection of the weak-field metric reduces at first order to the gradient
of the potential, and its geodesics follow Newton's orbits. The proposition records both facts, which are shown in
@fig-newtonian-limit.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-newtonian-limit}
#### The Newtonian limit of the Christoffel symbols

For $g_{tt} = 1 + 2\Phi$, $g_{ij} = -(1 - 2\Phi)\delta_{ij}$ with $\Phi = -M/r$, the Levi-Civita connection has
$\Gamma^i_{tt} = \partial_i\Phi + O(\Phi^2)$ for $i = x, y, z$, and the geodesic of the weak-field metric with $M =
10^{-3}$ stays within $0.05$ of the Newtonian orbit over about two periods.
:::

The orbit in @fig-newtonian-limit starts at $(1, 0)$ with a speed below that of a circular orbit. This makes the
starting point the aphelion of an ellipse.

::: {#exm-gr-nl-orbit-data}
#### The orbit of the figure

With $M = 10^{-3}$ the circular speed at $r = 1$ is $\sqrt{M/r} \approx 0.0316$; the initial speed $0.028$ is smaller,
so the orbit is an ellipse with aphelion at $x = 1$. Its angular momentum $0.028$ gives the semi-latus rectum $p = 0.
028^2/M = 0.784$, hence eccentricity $e = 1 - p = 0.216$, semi-major axis $a = p/(1 - e^2) = 0.82$ and perihelion
$0.64$ (@prp-clm-kepler-orbits); along it $|\Phi| \leq 1.6 \times 10^{-3}$, deep in the weak-field regime of
@def-newtonian-limit.
:::

The proposition keeps only the first order in $\Phi$. The exact symbols differ by factors of $1 \pm 2\Phi$, which
the next example displays.

::: {#exm-gr-nl-exact}
#### The exact symbols

For the weak-field metric the exact symbols are $\Gamma^i_{tt} = \partial_i\Phi/(1 - 2\Phi)$ and $\Gamma^t_{ti} =
\partial_i\Phi/(1 + 2\Phi)$ (@exr-gr-nl-exact-christoffel): the corrections are of relative size $\Phi \sim 10^{-3}$ on
the orbit of the figure, and they produce the slow precession seen in the deviation of the two curves.
:::

The geodesic equation also has spatial Christoffel symbols $\Gamma^i_{jk}$ from $g_{ij}$. They multiply two powers
of the velocity and so drop out for slow particles, but not for light.

::: {#exm-gr-nl-velocity-terms}
#### Terms that need speed

$\Gamma^x_{yy} = \partial_x\Phi/(1 - 2\Phi)$ enters the geodesic equation as $\Gamma^x_{yy}\dot y^2$, of order $\Phi v^2$:
negligible against $\Gamma^x_{tt} \sim \Phi$ when $v \ll 1$, but of the same order for light, $v = 1$. This is why
the deflection of light is twice the Newtonian value (@exr-gr-nl-light).
:::

The weak-field metric also predicts the colour of light from the Sun. The next example evaluates the shift of a solar
spectral line as seen from the Earth, where two potentials enter.

::: {#exm-grb-solar-lines}
#### Spectral lines from the Sun

A line emitted at the solar surface $R$ and received at the distance $d$ of the Earth is shifted by $\Delta\nu/\nu =
\Phi(R) - \Phi(d) = -\tfrac{GM}{c^2}\bigl(\tfrac1R - \tfrac1d\bigr)$, to first order in $\Phi$. With $GM/c^2 = 1.49\,$km, $R = 7.8 \times 10^8\,$m and
$d = 1.5 \times 10^{11}\,$m this is $-1.91 \times 10^{-6} + 0.01 \times 10^{-6} = -1.90 \times 10^{-6}$: a redshift, dominated by the solar
potential, the potential of the Sun at the Earth correcting it by half a percent [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 2.125].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
A circular orbit is the simplest check of the proposition. The first exercise compares its speed and period in the
weak-field metric with Newton's.

::: {#exr-gr-nl-circular}
#### A circular orbit

Using $\ddot x^i = -\partial_i\Phi$ with $\Phi = -M/r$, find the speed and period of a circular orbit of radius $r$, and
evaluate them for $M = 10^{-3}$, $r = 1$. How many revolutions of the plotted ellipse (@exm-gr-nl-orbit-data) fit into
the time span $300$ of @fig-newtonian-limit?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$v^2/r = M/r^2$ gives $v = \sqrt{M/r} = 0.0316$ and $T = 2\pi r/v = 2\pi r^{3/2}/\sqrt M \approx 199$. The plotted
ellipse has aphelion $1$ and semi-major axis $a = 0.82$; by Kepler's third law (@prp-clm-kepler-orbits) its period is
$2\pi a^{3/2}/\sqrt M \approx 148$, so the time $300$ covers about two revolutions.
:::

The exact Christoffel symbols of the weak-field metric can be found for an arbitrary potential. The second exercise
does this with SageManifolds.

::: {#exr-gr-nl-exact-christoffel}
#### The exact Christoffel symbols

For $g_{tt} = 1 + 2\Phi$, $g_{ij} = -(1 - 2\Phi)\delta_{ij}$ with an arbitrary static $\Phi(x, y, z)$, compute
$\Gamma^i_{tt}$, $\Gamma^t_{ti}$ and $\Gamma^x_{yy}$ exactly.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\Gamma^i_{tt} = -\tfrac12g^{ii}\partial_ig_{tt} = \partial_i\Phi/(1 - 2\Phi)$, $\Gamma^t_{ti} = \tfrac12g^{tt}\partial_ig_{tt} =
\partial_i\Phi/(1 + 2\Phi)$ and $\Gamma^x_{yy} = -\tfrac12g^{xx}\partial_xg_{yy} = \partial_x\Phi/(1 - 2\Phi)$; to first order
the first two are $\partial_i\Phi$, as in @prp-newtonian-limit.

{{< sage exr-gr-nl-exact-christoffel >}}
:::

Light is never slow, so the Newtonian limit does not apply to it directly. The third exercise compares the
deflection of a light ray computed in two ways.

::: {#exr-gr-nl-light}
#### Light in a weak field

A Newtonian particle passing a mass $M$ at speed $1$ and impact parameter $b$ is deflected by $2GM/b$. Using
@exm-gr-nl-velocity-terms, explain why the deflection of light in the weak-field metric is twice this.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For the Newtonian particle the transverse acceleration is $-\partial_\perp\Phi$ and $\int\partial_\perp\Phi\,dt = 2GM/b$
along the straight line. For light, $\dot x^2 = 1$ and the spatial symbols contribute $\Gamma^\perp_{xx}\dot x^2 =
\partial_\perp\Phi$ as well, an equal amount: the time and space parts of the metric bend the ray equally, and the
total deflection is $4GM/b$. In terms of the metric, light feels $g_{tt}$ and $g_{ij}$ together, the slow particle only
$g_{tt}$. The full Schwarzschild computation is @prp-gr-schwarzschild.
:::

Real signals are shifted by gravity and by motion at once. The next exercise compares the two effects for a signal from a
rocket, using the book's data, and asks which one dominates.

::: {#exr-grb-rocket-signal}
#### A signal from a rising rocket

A spaceship rising radially at $v = 0.1\,$km/s at an altitude of $1000\,$km sends a light signal to the ground. With Sage, compute the
gravitational and the Doppler shifts to lowest order, with $GM_\oplus = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 5.98 \times 10^{24}\,\mathrm{m^3/s^2}$ and $R_\oplus =
6.3 \times 10^3\,$km. Which effect dominates? [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 2.126]
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The light falls from $R_\oplus + h$ to $R_\oplus$ and is blueshifted by $\tfrac{GM}{c^2}\bigl(\tfrac{1}{R_\oplus} - \tfrac{1}{R_\oplus + h}\bigr)$; the source recedes, which
redshifts it by $v/c$:

{{< sage exr-grb-rocket-signal >}}

The Doppler shift is larger by a factor of about $3500$: a rocket would have to rise at about $3\,$cm/s for the two to cancel.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

### The action

The dynamics of the metric itself comes from an action, as for every field of @sec-actions. Coordinate invariance
and the requirement of at most two derivatives leave essentially one candidate, the integral of the scalar curvature.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-einstein-hilbert-action}
#### Einstein-Hilbert action

The **Einstein-Hilbert action** is
$$
S_{\mathrm{EH}}[g] = -\frac{1}{2\kappa^2}\int d^4x\,\sqrt{-g}\,R, \qquad \kappa^2 = 8\pi G,
$$ {#eq-einstein-hilbert}
with $R$ the scalar curvature (@def-scalar-curvature) and $\sqrt{-g}\,d^4x$ the volume element
(@def-volume-element); the overall sign is the one that makes the kinetic energy of the graviton positive in our
signature $(+, -, -, -)$, in which $R$ has the opposite sign to the mostly-plus $R$ of @carroll1997
(@sec-conventions-indices). It is the only action built from the metric alone with at most two derivatives, up to
the addition of a constant, the cosmological term $-\tfrac{1}{\kappa^2}\int\sqrt{-g}\,\Lambda$, whose sign is the
same in both signatures [@carroll1997, eqs. 4.54-4.55 and 4.73]. @carroll1997 writes $S = \tfrac{1}{8\pi G}S_H +
S_M$ with $S_H = \int\sqrt{-g}R$ [eq. 4.68] in his signature; after conversion this is a factor $2$ different from
@eq-einstein-hilbert, compensated in his definition of the stress tensor.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
In two dimensions the action is special: it does not depend on the metric at all. The sphere shows this most
directly.

::: {#exm-eh-sphere}
#### The action of a sphere

For the unit sphere, $R = 2$ (@prp-sphere-riemann) and $\int\sqrt g\,d^2x = 4\pi$, so $\int\sqrt gR = 8\pi = 4\pi\chi$:
in two dimensions the Einstein-Hilbert action is the topological invariant of the Gauss-Bonnet theorem
(@exr-gauss-bonnet) and has no equations of motion, which is why the Einstein tensor vanishes identically there
(@exm-einstein-tensor-2d).
:::

The same action in five dimensions is the starting point of the main theme. Its evaluation on a product metric is a
long but purely geometric computation.

::: {#exm-eh-kk}
#### The action of Kaluza-Klein theory

Part III starts from @eq-einstein-hilbert in five dimensions, $S = -\tfrac{1}{2\hat\kappa^2}\int d^5x\sqrt{-\hat g}\,
\hat R$, and shows that for a metric of the product form $M_4 \times S^1$ it equals the four-dimensional
Einstein-Hilbert action plus Maxwell's action @eq-maxwell-action plus a scalar's: everything in that computation
is the geometry of Part I applied to a $5 \times 5$ metric.
:::

Other invariants of the curvature exist, but they bring more derivatives. They are the first corrections of an
effective theory rather than part of classical general relativity.

::: {#exm-eh-higher-derivative}
#### Higher-derivative actions

$\int\sqrt{-g}\,R^2$ and $\int\sqrt{-g}\,R_{\mu\nu}R^{\mu\nu}$ are also coordinate invariant but contain four
derivatives of the metric; they are suppressed by inverse powers of a high scale in the effective theories of
@def-renormalisation and are absent from the classical reductions of Parts III to V.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The action contains Newton's constant, which has dimensions in natural units. The first exercise works out these
dimensions and the mass scale they define.

::: {#exr-gr-eh-dimension}
#### The Planck mass

In units $\hbar = c = 1$, find the mass dimension of $G$ from the requirement that @eq-einstein-hilbert be
dimensionless, define the Planck mass $M_P = G^{-1/2}$ and evaluate it in GeV using $G = 6.71 \times
10^{-39}\,\mathrm{GeV^{-2}}$. What is the dimension of $G$ in $n$ spacetime dimensions?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$d^4x$ has mass dimension $-4$ and $R$, two derivatives of the dimensionless metric, has dimension $2$; so $1/G$
must have dimension $2$, $[G] = -2$. Then $M_P = (6.71 \times 10^{-39})^{-1/2}\,\mathrm{GeV} = 1.22 \times 10^{19}\,
\mathrm{GeV}$, the scale at which quantum gravity becomes strong. In $n$ dimensions $d^nx\,R$ has dimension $2 - n$,
so $[G_n] = 2 - n$; this is why a higher-dimensional Newton constant is related to the four-dimensional one by a volume.
:::

The second exercise, from the old version of this section, confirms that the two-dimensional action is
topological. It uses the Gauss-Bonnet theorem of @sec-ricci.

::: {#exr-eh-topological}
#### Two dimensions

Compute $\int\sqrt g\,R$ for the torus of @exm-riemann-torus and for the sphere of radius $a$, and explain why the
result does not depend on $a$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For the sphere of radius $a$, $R = 2/a^2$ and the area is $4\pi a^2$, so $\int\sqrt gR = 8\pi$, independent of $a$;
for the torus the integral of the Gaussian curvature vanishes (@prp-gauss-bonnet-examples), so $\int\sqrt gR = 0$.
Both are $4\pi\chi$ by the Gauss-Bonnet theorem: in two dimensions the Einstein-Hilbert action is a topological
invariant, with no dependence on the metric and hence no equations of motion.
:::

On a solution of the equations with cosmological constant the integrand of the action takes a definite value. The
third exercise evaluates it on de Sitter space with SageManifolds.

::: {#exr-gr-eh-de-sitter-density}
#### The action density of de Sitter space

For $ds^2 = dt^2 - e^{2Ht}d\vec x^2$ in four dimensions compute $\sqrt{-g}$, $R$ and the Lagrangian density
$\sqrt{-g}\,(R + 2\Lambda)$ of the action of @def-cosmological-constant at $\Lambda = 3H^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\sqrt{-g} = e^{3Ht}$, $R = -12H^2$ (@exr-de-sitter-4d), so $\sqrt{-g}\,(R + 2\Lambda) = -6H^2e^{3Ht}$. On a vacuum solution
in four dimensions $R = -4\Lambda$ (@exr-gr-vacuum-trace), so the density is always $-2\Lambda\sqrt{-g}$: the on-shell
action is minus twice the cosmological term, proportional to the spacetime volume.

{{< sage exr-gr-eh-de-sitter-density >}}
:::
::::

To derive equations of motion from @eq-einstein-hilbert we must vary the metric, and both the volume element and
the curvature respond. The next definition fixes what a variation is and records the two identities that compute
the response.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-metric-variation}
#### Variation of the metric

A **variation of the metric** is a one-parameter family $g_{\mu\nu} + \epsilon\,\delta g_{\mu\nu}$, equivalently
$g^{\mu\nu} + \epsilon\,\delta g^{\mu\nu}$ with $\delta g^{\mu\nu} = -g^{\mu\rho}g^{\nu\sigma}\delta g_{\rho\sigma}$
(because $\delta(g^{\mu\nu}g_{\nu\rho}) = 0$). Two identities govern how the action responds: for the determinant,
$$
\delta\sqrt{-g} = -\tfrac12\sqrt{-g}\,g_{\mu\nu}\,\delta g^{\mu\nu}
$$ {#eq-delta-sqrt-g}
from $\delta\det M = \det M\operatorname{tr}(M^{-1}\delta M)$ [@carroll1997, eqs. 4.62-4.65; @exr-eh-variation], and for
the curvature the **Palatini identity**
$$
\delta R^\rho{}_{\sigma\mu\nu} = \nabla_\mu(\delta\Gamma^\rho_{\nu\sigma}) - \nabla_\nu(\delta\Gamma^\rho_{\mu\sigma}),
\qquad
\delta R_{\mu\nu} = \nabla_\rho(\delta\Gamma^\rho_{\nu\mu}) - \nabla_\nu(\delta\Gamma^\rho_{\rho\mu}),
$$ {#eq-palatini}
which holds because $\delta\Gamma$, the difference of two connections, is a tensor [@carroll1997, eqs. 4.59-4.60;
@exr-palatini].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For a diagonal metric the determinant identity can be checked by hand. The example does this; the general case is
the subject of @exr-eh-variation.

::: {#exm-variation-diagonal}
#### A diagonal metric

For $g = \operatorname{diag}(g_0, g_1, g_2, g_3)$, $\sqrt{-g} = \sqrt{-g_0g_1g_2g_3}$ and varying $g^{\mu\mu} \to g^{\mu\mu} +
\epsilon d_\mu$ gives $\tfrac{d}{d\epsilon}\sqrt{-g} = -\tfrac12\sqrt{-g}\sum_\mu g_\mu d_\mu$, which is
@eq-delta-sqrt-g; the same holds for a non-diagonal metric (@exr-eh-variation).
:::

A variation proportional to the metric itself is a change of scale. It shows how the dimension of spacetime enters
the variation of the volume.

::: {#exm-variation-conformal}
#### A conformal rescaling

$\delta g_{\mu\nu} = 2\sigma g_{\mu\nu}$ gives $\delta g^{\mu\nu} = -2\sigma g^{\mu\nu}$ and $\delta\sqrt{-g} =
4\sigma\sqrt{-g}$ in four dimensions: the volume element scales with the fourth power of the length scale, as it
must. In $n$ dimensions the factor is $n\sigma$, which is how the dimension enters the reductions of Part III.
:::

The variation of the Ricci tensor enters the action contracted with the inverse metric. The contraction turns it
into a total derivative, which is the key step of the derivation of the Einstein equations.

::: {#exm-variation-divergence}
#### The curvature variation is a divergence

Contracting @eq-palatini with $g^{\mu\nu}$, which commutes with $\nabla$ by @eq-metric-compatibility, gives
$g^{\mu\nu}\delta R_{\mu\nu} = \nabla_\sigma V^\sigma$ with $V^\sigma = g^{\mu\nu}\delta\Gamma^\sigma_{\nu\mu} -
g^{\mu\sigma}\delta\Gamma^\rho_{\rho\mu}$, and $\int\sqrt{-g}\,\nabla_\sigma V^\sigma = \int\partial_\sigma(\sqrt{-g}V^\sigma)$
vanishes for variations that vanish at infinity [@carroll1997, eq. 4.61]: this term contributes nothing to the
equations of motion, which is what makes them second order.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The inverse metric varies with a minus sign and two metric factors. The first exercise checks this rule on a general
symmetric matrix.

::: {#exr-gr-variation-inverse}
#### Varying the inverse

Show that $\delta g^{\mu\nu} = -g^{\mu\rho}g^{\nu\sigma}\delta g_{\rho\sigma}$ by differentiating $(g + \epsilon\,\delta g)^{-1}$ at
$\epsilon = 0$, and check it for a general symmetric $3 \times 3$ matrix.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Differentiating $(g + \epsilon\,\delta g)(g + \epsilon\,\delta g)^{-1} = 1$ gives $\delta g\,g^{-1} + g\,\delta(g^{-1}) = 0$, so
$\delta(g^{-1}) = -g^{-1}\,\delta g\,g^{-1}$, which in components is the stated formula. In Sage, with all six entries of
$g$ and of $\delta g$ symbolic:

{{< sage exr-gr-variation-inverse >}}
:::

The determinant identity is the second piece of the variation. The second exercise, kept from the old version of the
section, checks it first on a diagonal metric and then in general.

::: {#exr-eh-variation}
#### The variation of the determinant

Verify @eq-delta-sqrt-g on a diagonal metric by differentiating $\sqrt{-\det g}$ with respect to a variation of
the inverse metric, then on a general symmetric $2 \times 2$ metric.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For $g = \operatorname{diag}(g_0, g_1, g_2, g_3)$, $g^{\mu\mu} = 1/g_\mu$; varying $g^{\mu\mu} \to g^{\mu\mu} + \epsilon
d_\mu$ changes $g_\mu$ to $1/(1/g_\mu + \epsilon d_\mu)$, and differentiating at $\epsilon = 0$ gives
$-\tfrac12\sqrt{-g}\sum_\mu g_\mu d_\mu$. For a general metric, $g_{\mu\nu}\delta g^{\mu\nu} = \operatorname{tr}(g\,\delta
g^{-1})$. In Sage:

{{< sage exr-eh-variation >}}
:::

The Palatini identity rests on the fact that the difference of two connections is a tensor. The third exercise
proves this and derives the identity.

::: {#exr-palatini}
#### The variation of the connection is a tensor

Show that $\delta\Gamma^\rho_{\mu\nu}$ transforms as a tensor although $\Gamma^\rho_{\mu\nu}$ does not, and derive
the first formula of @eq-palatini.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Under a coordinate change the Christoffel symbols @eq-christoffel transform with an inhomogeneous term
$\tfrac{\partial x^\rho}{\partial x'^\lambda}\tfrac{\partial^2x'^\lambda}{\partial x^\mu\partial x^\nu}$ that does not depend on
the metric; the difference of the symbols of $g + \epsilon\delta g$ and of $g$ has this term cancel, so
$\delta\Gamma$ is a tensor. Varying @eq-riemann, $\delta R^\rho{}_{\sigma\mu\nu} = \partial_\mu\delta\Gamma^\rho_{\nu\sigma} -
\partial_\nu\delta\Gamma^\rho_{\mu\sigma} + \delta\Gamma^\rho_{\mu\lambda}\Gamma^\lambda_{\nu\sigma} + \Gamma^\rho_{\mu\lambda}
\delta\Gamma^\lambda_{\nu\sigma} - (\mu \leftrightarrow \nu)$; writing out $\nabla_\mu(\delta\Gamma^\rho_{\nu\sigma}) -
\nabla_\nu(\delta\Gamma^\rho_{\mu\sigma})$ with the covariant derivative of a $(1, 2)$ tensor
(@def-covariant-derivative-tensor) reproduces exactly these terms, the $\Gamma\delta\Gamma$ terms with the lower
index $\lambda$ cancelling by the symmetry of $\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu}$.
:::
::::

## The Einstein equations {#sec-einstein-equations}

Varying the Einstein-Hilbert action with the two identities of @sec-einstein-hilbert gives the Einstein tensor,
and adding matter gives the Einstein equations. This section carries the variation out in full, defines the
stress tensor and the cosmological constant, and checks the equations on two explicit metrics: the sphere, where
the Einstein tensor vanishes identically, and de Sitter space, the simplest curved solution, computed in full in
three dimensions and, in an exercise, in four. Both return in Part VI, where internal spheres and de Sitter or anti-de
Sitter spacetimes are the vacua of supergravity compactifications.

### The variation of the action

Matter enters the Einstein equations through a single symmetric tensor. It is defined as the response of the matter
action to a change of the metric, which makes it automatically covariant.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-stress-tensor}
#### Stress tensor

The **stress tensor** (energy-momentum tensor) of matter with action $S_M[g, \text{fields}]$ is
$$
T_{\mu\nu} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{-g}}\frac{\delta S_M}{\delta g^{\mu\nu}},
$$ {#eq-stress-tensor}
a symmetric tensor field conserved on the matter equations of motion, $\nabla^\mu T_{\mu\nu} = 0$; on flat space
it agrees with the Noether current of translations (@prp-energy-momentum) up to terms that do not change the
conserved charges [@carroll1997, eq. 4.70, with his normalisation and the opposite overall sign, which comes with
his signature]. The sign is fixed by requiring $T_{tt} \geq 0$ for a scalar field (@exm-stress-scalar).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The scalar field is the simplest matter, and its stress tensor shows the general pattern. The time component is the
familiar energy density.

::: {#exm-stress-scalar}
#### A scalar field

For $S_M = \int\sqrt{-g}\,(\tfrac12g^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu\phi\partial_\nu\phi - V)$, @eq-delta-sqrt-g gives
$T_{\mu\nu} = \partial_\mu\phi\partial_\nu\phi - g_{\mu\nu}(\tfrac12(\partial\phi)^2 - V)$, whose $tt$ component is the energy
density $\tfrac12\dot\phi^2 + \tfrac12(\nabla\phi)^2 + V$ (@exr-stress-scalar).
:::

The electromagnetic field is the classic example of a traceless stress tensor. Its energy density and its
momentum density, the Poynting vector, follow from the same formula (@exr-gr-maxwell-stress).

::: {#exm-stress-maxwell}
#### The electromagnetic field

For the Maxwell action @eq-maxwell-action, $T_{\mu\nu} = F_{\mu\rho}F^\rho{}_\nu + \tfrac14g_{\mu\nu}F_{\rho\sigma}F^{\rho\sigma}$,
traceless in four dimensions, with $T_{tt} = \tfrac12(\vec E^2 + \vec B^2)$: the energy density of the field.
:::

On large scales matter is described by a density and a pressure rather than by individual fields. The perfect fluid
packages them into a tensor and is the source used in cosmology.

::: {#exm-stress-fluid}
#### A perfect fluid

$T_{\mu\nu} = (\rho + p)u_\mu u_\nu - pg_{\mu\nu}$ with four-velocity $u^\mu$ ($u_\mu u^\mu = 1$), density $\rho$ and pressure $p$ is the
stress tensor of cosmology; static dust has $p = 0$ and $T_{tt} = \rho$, the source of the Newtonian limit
(@exr-newton-constant).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The trace of the stress tensor appears in the trace-reversed Einstein equations. The first exercise computes it for
the perfect fluid and its standard special cases.

::: {#exr-gr-fluid-trace}
#### The trace of a perfect fluid

Compute $T = g^{\mu\nu}T_{\mu\nu}$ for the perfect fluid of @exm-stress-fluid. For which equation of state $p = w\rho$ does
it vanish, and which of the examples of this section has that equation of state?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$T = (\rho + p)u_\mu u^\mu - 4p = \rho - 3p$. It vanishes for $w = \tfrac13$, radiation, consistent with the traceless
Maxwell tensor of @exm-stress-maxwell: a gas of photons is a perfect fluid with $p = \rho/3$. Dust has $T = \rho$ and a
cosmological constant ($w = -1$) has $T = 4\rho$.
:::

The second exercise, from the old version of this section, derives the scalar stress tensor from @eq-stress-tensor
and compares it with the Noether tensor of flat space. The two agree, which justifies calling @eq-stress-tensor the
energy-momentum tensor.

::: {#exr-stress-scalar}
#### The stress tensor of a scalar

Derive $T_{\mu\nu}$ for $S_M = \int\sqrt{-g}\,(\tfrac12g^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu\phi\partial_\nu\phi - V)$ from
@eq-stress-tensor and compare with the Noether tensor of @prp-energy-momentum on flat space.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\delta S_M = \int\sqrt{-g}\,[\tfrac12\partial_\mu\phi\partial_\nu\phi\,\delta g^{\mu\nu}] + \int\delta\sqrt{-g}\,\mathcal{L}$ with
$\delta\sqrt{-g} = -\tfrac12\sqrt{-g}g_{\mu\nu}\delta g^{\mu\nu}$, so $T_{\mu\nu} = \tfrac{2}{\sqrt{-g}}\tfrac{\delta S_M}
{\delta g^{\mu\nu}} = \partial_\mu\phi\partial_\nu\phi - g_{\mu\nu}\mathcal{L}$. On flat space with $V = \tfrac12m^2\phi^2$ this
is exactly $T^{\mu\nu} = \partial^\mu\phi\partial^\nu\phi - \eta^{\mu\nu}\mathcal{L}$ of @prp-energy-momentum.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** The divergence of the flat-space tensor is the Lean-verified statement of @prp-energy-momentum (see its
Verification box).

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The Maxwell stress tensor can be checked component by component. The third exercise does this in Sage for an
arbitrary electric and magnetic field.

::: {#exr-gr-maxwell-stress}
#### The Maxwell stress tensor in components

On flat space put $F_{0i} = E_i$ and $F_{ij} = -\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$. Show that $F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu} = 2(\vec B^2 - \vec E^2)$ and
that the tensor of @exm-stress-maxwell has $T_{00} = \tfrac12(\vec E^2 + \vec B^2)$, $T^{0i} = (\vec E \times \vec B)_i$ and zero
trace.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu} = 2F_{0i}F^{0i} + F_{ij}F^{ij} = -2\vec E^2 + 2\vec B^2$ since raising one time and one space index
gives a minus sign. Then $T_{00} = F_{0i}F^i{}_0 + \tfrac14F^2 = \vec E^2 + \tfrac12(\vec B^2 - \vec E^2)$, the energy
density; the mixed components give the Poynting vector, and the trace $F_{\mu\rho}F^{\rho\mu} + F^2 = -F^2 + F^2 = 0$.

{{< sage exr-gr-maxwell-stress >}}
:::

Conservation of the stress tensor is the relativistic form of the equations of fluid dynamics. The next exercise
recovers the Newtonian continuity and Euler equations from it, gravity included.

::: {#exr-grb-newtonian-fluid}
#### The Euler equations from $\nabla_\mu T^{\mu\nu} = 0$

For the perfect fluid $T^{\mu\nu} = (\rho + p)u^\mu u^\nu - pg^{\mu\nu}$ in the weak-field metric of @def-newtonian-limit, with $u^\mu \approx (1, \vec v)$,
$|\vec v| \ll 1$ and $p \ll \rho$, show that the $\nu = t$ component of $\nabla_\mu T^{\mu\nu} = 0$ is the continuity equation $\partial_t\rho +
\nabla\cdot(\rho\vec v) = 0$ and the spatial components are the Euler equation $\rho(\partial_t + \vec v\cdot\nabla)\vec v = -\nabla p - \rho\nabla\Phi$
[@plebanski2024introduction, Sec. 12.19, Exercises 1-2].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\nabla_\mu T^{\mu\nu} = \partial_\mu T^{\mu\nu} + \Gamma^\mu_{\mu\lambda}T^{\lambda\nu} + \Gamma^\nu_{\mu\lambda}T^{\mu\lambda}$. To lowest order $T^{tt} = \rho$, $T^{ti} = \rho v^i$, $T^{ij} =
\rho v^iv^j + p\delta^{ij}$ (since $g^{ij} \approx -\delta^{ij}$), and the only Christoffel symbol multiplying the large component $T^{tt}$ is
$\Gamma^i_{tt} = \partial_i\Phi$ (@prp-newtonian-limit); the others are of order $\Phi$ and multiply small terms. For $\nu = t$:
$\partial_t\rho + \partial_i(\rho v^i) = 0$. For $\nu = i$: $\partial_t(\rho v^i) + \partial_j(\rho v^iv^j) + \partial_ip + \rho\partial_i\Phi = 0$; subtracting $v^i$ times
the continuity equation leaves $\rho(\partial_tv^i + v^j\partial_jv^i) = -\partial_ip - \rho\partial_i\Phi$. For dust, $p = 0$, this is the geodesic equation of
@exr-gr-dust-geodesic in Newtonian form.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

With the stress tensor in hand the field equations can be stated. They equate the Einstein tensor of
@def-einstein-tensor, built from the curvature, to the stress tensor of the matter.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-einstein-equations}
#### Einstein equations

The **Einstein equations** are the equations of motion of $S_{\mathrm{EH}} + S_M$ under variations of the
metric,
$$
G_{\mu\nu} = \kappa^2T_{\mu\nu}, \qquad G_{\mu\nu} = R_{\mu\nu} - \tfrac12R\,g_{\mu\nu},
$$ {#eq-einstein-equations}
with $G_{\mu\nu}$ the Einstein tensor of @def-einstein-tensor and $\kappa^2 = 8\pi G$ fixed by the Newtonian limit
(@prp-eh-variation-text). Their trace, $-R = \kappa^2T$ in four dimensions, gives the **trace-reversed form**
$R_{\mu\nu} = \kappa^2(T_{\mu\nu} - \tfrac12Tg_{\mu\nu})$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first check of the equations is that they contain Newton's law of gravitation. This also fixes the constant
$\kappa$.

::: {#exm-einstein-newton}
#### The Newtonian limit of the equations

For static dust with $T_{tt} = \rho$, $T = \rho$, the trace-reversed equation gives $R_{tt} = \tfrac12\kappa^2\rho$;
with $R_{tt} = \nabla^2\Phi$ in the weak-field metric this is Poisson's equation $\nabla^2\Phi = 4\pi G\rho$ exactly
when $\kappa^2 = 8\pi G$ [@carroll1997, eqs. 4.46-4.52] (@exr-newton-constant).
:::

In two dimensions the Einstein tensor vanishes for every metric. The equations then say nothing at all, in line
with the topological action.

::: {#exm-einstein-two-dimensions}
#### Two dimensions

In two dimensions $G_{ij} \equiv 0$ for every metric (@exm-einstein-tensor-2d, @prp-einstein-2d): the Einstein
equations are empty, consistent with the action being topological (@exr-eh-topological), and two-dimensional
gravity needs a different action.
:::

In five dimensions the equations contain more than gravity. This observation, that one geometric equation contains
several four-dimensional field equations, is what starts the main theme.

::: {#exm-einstein-kk}
#### The Kaluza-Klein equations

The five-dimensional vacuum Einstein equations $\hat G_{MN} = 0$ on $M_4 \times S^1$ split, in Part III, into the
four-dimensional Einstein equations sourced by the Maxwell stress tensor of @exm-stress-maxwell and a scalar,
Maxwell's equations, and the equation of the scalar: gravity in five dimensions is gravity plus electromagnetism
in four.
:::

In vacuum the linearised equations of the weak-field exercise become a wave equation, and its solutions are
gravitational waves. The next example counts their physical components, which shows that a gravitational wave, like
light, has two polarisations.

::: {#exm-grb-gw-polarisations}
#### Two polarisations

Write $g_{\mu\nu} = \eta_{\mu\nu} + h_{\mu\nu}$ with $|h_{\mu\nu}| \ll 1$. Of the ten components of $h_{\mu\nu}$, a coordinate change $x^\mu \to x^\mu + \chi^\mu$ removes
four, and in vacuum the residual freedom of the Lorenz gauge removes four more. In the transverse traceless gauge $h_{0\mu} = 0$,
$\eta^{\mu\nu}h_{\mu\nu} = 0$, $\partial_jh_{ij} = 0$, a wave travelling along $z$ has only
$$
h_{xx} = -h_{yy} = h_+, \qquad h_{xy} = h_{yx} = h_\times ,
$$
two independent components, the plus and cross polarisations, rotated into each other by $45°$ rotations about $z$
[@blennow2022relativity, Problem 2.133].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The polarisations act on matter by changing proper distances. The second example computes the change for two free
particles on the $x$-axis, the effect that interferometric detectors measure.

::: {#exm-grb-gw-ruler}
#### A wave stretches a ruler

Let $h_+ = h_0\sin(2\pi f(t - z))$, $h_\times = 0$, and let two free particles sit at $x = 0$ and $x = L$ on the $x$-axis. In the transverse
traceless gauge free particles initially at rest keep their coordinates, and the proper distance between them at time $t$ is
$$
d = \int_0^L\sqrt{-g_{xx}}\,dx = \sqrt{1 - h_+}\,L \approx \Bigl(1 - \tfrac12h_0\sin(2\pi ft)\Bigr)L ,
$$
oscillating with relative amplitude $h_0/2$, while distances along $y$ oscillate in antiphase. For $h_0 = 10^{-21}$ and $L = 4\,$km
the change is $2 \times 10^{-18}\,$m, a thousandth of a proton radius [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 2.133].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The trace-reversed form is often the more convenient one, especially in vacuum. The first exercise derives it in
any dimension.

::: {#exr-gr-trace-reversed}
#### The trace-reversed equations

Show that in $n \geq 3$ dimensions $G_{\mu\nu} = \kappa^2T_{\mu\nu}$ is equivalent to $R_{\mu\nu} = \kappa^2\bigl(T_{\mu\nu} -
\tfrac{1}{n - 2}T\,g_{\mu\nu}\bigr)$, and deduce that the vacuum equations are $R_{\mu\nu} = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The trace of $R_{\mu\nu} - \tfrac12Rg_{\mu\nu} = \kappa^2T_{\mu\nu}$ is $R(1 - n/2) = \kappa^2T$, so $R = -2\kappa^2T/(n - 2)$.
Substituting, $R_{\mu\nu} = \kappa^2T_{\mu\nu} + \tfrac12Rg_{\mu\nu} = \kappa^2(T_{\mu\nu} - Tg_{\mu\nu}/(n - 2))$; the steps reverse.
For $T_{\mu\nu} = 0$ this is $R_{\mu\nu} = 0$, Ricci flatness. For $n = 2$ the trace equation reads $0 = \kappa^2T$ and
the argument fails, as it must (@exm-einstein-two-dimensions).
:::

The second exercise, from the old version of this section, fixes $\kappa$ by the Newtonian limit. It uses the
trace-reversed equation with a dust source.

::: {#exr-newton-constant}
#### Fixing $\kappa$

Using $g_{tt} = 1 + 2\Phi$, $R_{tt} \approx \tfrac12\nabla^2h_{tt}$ and the trace-reversed Einstein equation with
$T_{tt} = \rho$, show that Poisson's equation $\nabla^2\Phi = 4\pi G\rho$ requires $\kappa^2 = 8\pi G$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For static dust, $T = g^{tt}T_{tt} = \rho$ and $T_{tt} - \tfrac12Tg_{tt} \approx \tfrac12\rho$, so $R_{tt} = \tfrac12\kappa^2\rho$.
With $h_{tt} = 2\Phi$, $R_{tt} \approx \partial_i\Gamma^i_{tt} = \tfrac12\nabla^2h_{tt} = \nabla^2\Phi$, hence $\nabla^2\Phi =
\tfrac12\kappa^2\rho$, and comparison with Poisson's equation gives $\kappa^2 = 8\pi G$ [@carroll1997, eqs. 4.46-4.52,
in his signature].
:::

The approximation $R_{tt} \approx \nabla^2\Phi$ used above deserves a direct test. The third exercise computes the
Einstein tensor of the weak-field metric to first order.

::: {#exr-gr-einstein-weak-field}
#### The weak-field Einstein tensor

For $g_{tt} = 1 + 2\Phi$, $g_{ij} = -(1 - 2\Phi)\delta_{ij}$ with static $\Phi$, compute $R_{tt}$ and $G_{tt}$ to first order in
$\Phi$, and show that $G_{tt} = \kappa^2\rho$ is Poisson's equation.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
To first order $R_{tt} = \nabla^2\Phi$ and $G_{tt} = 2\nabla^2\Phi$ (the spatial part of the metric contributes to
$G_{tt}$ through $R$). With $T_{tt} = \rho$, $2\nabla^2\Phi = \kappa^2\rho = 8\pi G\rho$, which is Poisson's equation
$\nabla^2\Phi = 4\pi G\rho$, in agreement with @exr-newton-constant.

{{< sage exr-gr-einstein-weak-field >}}
:::

The linearised theory has a gauge symmetry inherited from coordinate changes. The next exercise derives it and the
wave equation that it leads to, which underlies the two examples on gravitational waves.

::: {#exr-grb-linearised-gauge}
#### Linearised gauge symmetry

For $g_{\mu\nu} = \eta_{\mu\nu} + h_{\mu\nu}$, (a) show that to first order $R_{\mu\nu} = \tfrac12(\partial_\rho\partial_\mu h^\rho{}_\nu + \partial_\rho\partial_\nu h^\rho{}_\mu - \Box h_{\mu\nu} -
\partial_\mu\partial_\nu h)$, indices raised with $\eta$; (b) show that $x^\mu \to x^\mu + \chi^\mu$ with small $\chi$ changes $h_{\mu\nu}$ to $h_{\mu\nu} - \partial_\mu\chi_\nu -
\partial_\nu\chi_\mu$ and leaves $R_{\mu\nu}$ unchanged; (c) show that in the Lorenz gauge $\partial^\mu\bar h_{\mu\nu} = 0$, $\bar h_{\mu\nu} = h_{\mu\nu} -
\tfrac12\eta_{\mu\nu}h$, the vacuum equations are $\Box\bar h_{\mu\nu} = 0$ [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 2.112].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) To first order $\Gamma^\rho_{\nu\sigma} = \tfrac12(\partial_\nu h^\rho{}_\sigma + \partial_\sigma h^\rho{}_\nu - \partial^\rho h_{\nu\sigma})$ and the $\Gamma\Gamma$ terms of @eq-riemann-def are of
second order, so $R_{\sigma\nu} = \partial_\rho\Gamma^\rho_{\nu\sigma} - \partial_\nu\Gamma^\rho_{\rho\sigma}$ with $\Gamma^\rho_{\rho\sigma} = \tfrac12\partial_\sigma h$ gives the formula. (b) The
metric transforms as a tensor; to first order $g'_{\mu\nu}(x) = g_{\mu\nu}(x) - \partial_\mu\chi_\nu - \partial_\nu\chi_\mu$. Substituting $h \to h - 2\partial\cdot\chi$
in (a), the terms $\partial_\rho\partial_\mu\partial^\rho\chi_\nu$ cancel against those of $\Box$, and the remaining $\partial_\mu\partial_\nu\partial\cdot\chi$ cancel between the first,
second and fourth terms. (c) The gauge condition reads $\partial_\rho h^\rho{}_\nu = \tfrac12\partial_\nu h$, so the first two terms of (a) give
$\partial_\mu\partial_\nu h$, which cancels the last: $R_{\mu\nu} = -\tfrac12\Box h_{\mu\nu}$. In vacuum $R_{\mu\nu} = 0$, so $\Box h_{\mu\nu} = 0$, and taking the
trace $\Box h = 0$ and $\Box\bar h_{\mu\nu} = 0$. The gauge condition can always be reached by a $\chi$ with $\Box\chi_\nu = \partial^\mu\bar h_{\mu\nu}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

The Einstein equations were stated as a definition; the next proposition shows that they are the equations of motion
of the action. The computation combines the two identities of @def-metric-variation and drops a total derivative.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-eh-variation-text}
#### The Einstein equations from the action

Combining @eq-delta-sqrt-g, @eq-palatini and the vanishing of the divergence term (@exm-variation-divergence),
$$
\delta S_{\mathrm{EH}} = -\frac{1}{2\kappa^2}\int d^4x\,\sqrt{-g}\left(R_{\mu\nu} - \tfrac12R\,g_{\mu\nu}\right)\delta g^{\mu\nu},
$$ {#eq-eh-variation}
and stationarity of $S_{\mathrm{EH}} + S_M$ gives @eq-einstein-equations with the stress tensor @eq-stress-tensor.
The derivation follows @carroll1997 [eqs. 4.56-4.67]; the determinant identity is derived in @exr-eh-variation, and the
consistency $\nabla^\mu G_{\mu\nu} = 0 = \nabla^\mu T_{\mu\nu}$ follows from the contracted Bianchi identity of
@def-einstein-tensor.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending; the derivation is argued in the text (level `text`).

**Sage.** The determinant identity is checked symbolically in the solution of @exr-eh-variation.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The cosmological term varies only through the volume element. Its contribution is the first example of the
proposition at work.

::: {#exm-gr-variation-lambda}
#### Varying the cosmological term

With @eq-delta-sqrt-g, $\delta\int\sqrt{-g}\,2\Lambda = -\int\sqrt{-g}\,\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}\delta g^{\mu\nu}$, so the action
$-\tfrac{1}{2\kappa^2}\int\sqrt{-g}\,(R + 2\Lambda)$ varies into $-\tfrac{1}{2\kappa^2}\int\sqrt{-g}\,(G_{\mu\nu} - \Lambda g_{\mu\nu})
\delta g^{\mu\nu}$: the left-hand side of @def-cosmological-constant.
:::

The equations are consistent only if matter is conserved, because the Einstein tensor is divergence free. For the
scalar field the conservation is a consequence of its own equation of motion.

::: {#exm-gr-variation-bianchi}
#### Conservation from the field equation

For the scalar of @exm-stress-scalar, $\nabla^\mu T_{\mu\nu} = (\Box\phi + V'(\phi))\,\partial_\nu\phi$ with $\Box = \nabla^\mu\nabla_\mu$:
it vanishes when $\phi$ obeys its equation of motion $\Box\phi + V'(\phi) = 0$, so the contracted Bianchi identity
$\nabla^\mu G_{\mu\nu} = 0$ is respected.
:::

The derivation assumed that variations vanish at the boundary. On a manifold with boundary an extra term is needed,
which leaves the equations unchanged.

::: {#exm-gr-variation-boundary}
#### The boundary term

The total derivative of @exm-variation-divergence contains normal derivatives of $\delta g$, which do not vanish
when only $\delta g$ itself is fixed on the boundary. Adding the Gibbons-Hawking-York term, the integral over the
boundary of its extrinsic curvature, cancels them; it changes the value of the action, which matters in black hole
thermodynamics, but not the Einstein equations.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The relative sign of the gravitational and the matter actions decides whether gravity attracts. The first exercise
traces it through the variation.

::: {#exr-gr-variation-sign}
#### The sign of the coupling

Using @eq-eh-variation and $\delta S_M = \tfrac12\int\sqrt{-g}\,T_{\mu\nu}\delta g^{\mu\nu}$, derive $G_{\mu\nu} = \kappa^2T_{\mu\nu}$.
What equation would the opposite overall sign of @eq-einstein-hilbert give, and why is it unphysical?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\delta(S_{\mathrm{EH}} + S_M) = \int\sqrt{-g}\,\bigl(-\tfrac{1}{2\kappa^2}G_{\mu\nu} + \tfrac12T_{\mu\nu}\bigr)\delta g^{\mu\nu} = 0$ for
all $\delta g^{\mu\nu}$ gives $G_{\mu\nu} = \kappa^2T_{\mu\nu}$. With the opposite sign one would get $G_{\mu\nu} = -
\kappa^2T_{\mu\nu}$, whose Newtonian limit is $\nabla^2\Phi = -4\pi G\rho$: masses would repel, and the graviton would
have negative kinetic energy.
:::

Conservation of the stress tensor carries dynamical information. For dust it is the equation of motion of the dust
particles, as the second exercise shows.

::: {#exr-gr-dust-geodesic}
#### Dust moves on geodesics

For dust, $T^{\mu\nu} = \rho u^\mu u^\nu$ with $u_\mu u^\mu = 1$. Show that $\nabla_\mu T^{\mu\nu} = 0$ implies
$\nabla_\mu(\rho u^\mu) = 0$ and $u^\mu\nabla_\mu u^\nu = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\nabla_\mu T^{\mu\nu} = u^\nu\nabla_\mu(\rho u^\mu) + \rho u^\mu\nabla_\mu u^\nu$. Differentiating $u_\nu u^\nu = 1$ gives
$u_\nu u^\mu\nabla_\mu u^\nu = 0$, so contracting with $u_\nu$ leaves $\nabla_\mu(\rho u^\mu) = 0$, the conservation of
mass; the remaining term then gives $\rho u^\mu\nabla_\mu u^\nu = 0$, the geodesic equation (@def-geodesic). In general
relativity the motion of matter is not an extra postulate: it follows from the field equations through the Bianchi
identity.
:::

The action can be evaluated on a restricted family of metrics and varied within it. For a homogeneous universe this
gives the Friedmann equation directly, which the third exercise checks with SageManifolds.

::: {#exr-gr-variation-minisuperspace}
#### Minisuperspace

On $ds^2 = N(t)^2dt^2 - a(t)^2d\vec x^2$ take $S = -\tfrac{1}{2\kappa^2}\int\sqrt{-g}\,R - \int\sqrt{-g}\,\rho$ with dust,
$\rho a^3 = \rho_0$ constant. Vary with respect to the lapse $N$, set $N = 1$, and compare with
@def-gr-friedmann-equations.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Per unit coordinate volume the Lagrangian is $L = -\tfrac{1}{2\kappa^2}Na^3R - N\rho_0$. Its Euler-Lagrange derivative
with respect to $N$ at $N = 1$ is $3a\dot a^2/\kappa^2 - \rho_0$, so $\dot a^2/a^2 = \kappa^2\rho/3 = 8\pi G\rho/3$, the first
Friedmann equation. The lapse is the time-time component of the metric, and its equation is the $tt$ Einstein
equation, a constraint without second time derivatives.

{{< sage exr-gr-variation-minisuperspace >}}
:::
::::

### The cosmological constant and vacuum solutions

The action of @def-einstein-hilbert-action may contain a constant besides the curvature. This constant behaves like
an energy density of empty space, and it is the simplest explanation of the accelerated expansion of the universe.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-cosmological-constant}
#### Cosmological constant

The **cosmological constant** $\Lambda$ is the coefficient of the volume term in the action, $S = -\tfrac{1}{2\kappa^2}
\int\sqrt{-g}\,(R + 2\Lambda)$; it enters the equations as $G_{\mu\nu} - \Lambda g_{\mu\nu} = \kappa^2T_{\mu\nu}$, that
is as a stress tensor $T_{\mu\nu} = \tfrac{\Lambda}{\kappa^2}g_{\mu\nu}$ of constant energy density $T_{tt} =
\Lambda/\kappa^2$ and negative pressure [@carroll1997, eq. 8.29 and p. 125, in the signature $(-, +, +, +)$, where the
same $\Lambda$ appears as $G_{\mu\nu} + \Lambda g_{\mu\nu}$].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A constant potential energy of a field is indistinguishable from a cosmological constant. The example identifies the
two and relates their normalisations.

::: {#exm-lambda-vacuum-energy}
#### Vacuum energy

A constant potential $V_0$ in a scalar action contributes $T_{\mu\nu} = V_0g_{\mu\nu}$ by @exm-stress-scalar: a
cosmological constant $\Lambda = \kappa^2V_0$. The minimum value of the Higgs potential of @sec-higgs is of this
kind, which is why it is normalised to zero there.
:::

Compactified theories produce cosmological constants from the geometry of the internal space. The sign of the
contribution is opposite to the sign of the internal curvature.

::: {#exm-lambda-reduction}
#### Cosmological constants from reduction

Compactifying on a curved internal space produces a four-dimensional cosmological constant from the internal
curvature, $\Lambda \propto -R_{\text{int}}$ with $R_{\text{int}}$ the scalar curvature of the positive-definite
internal metric, which must be cancelled or compensated by fluxes (Part VI): the positive curvature of a sphere
alone gives a negative contribution.
:::

The sign of $\Lambda$ decides the large-scale geometry of the vacuum. The three cases have different names and
different physics.

::: {#exm-lambda-sign}
#### The three signs

$\Lambda > 0$ accelerates the expansion of the universe, as observed today; $\Lambda < 0$ gives anti-de Sitter
space, the setting of the AdS/CFT correspondence; $\Lambda = 0$ gives Minkowski space as the maximally symmetric
vacuum.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
A cosmological constant is a perfect fluid of a special kind, the same in every frame. The first exercise identifies
its pressure and its equation of state.

::: {#exr-gr-lambda-pressure}
#### Negative pressure

Write $T_{\mu\nu} = \tfrac{\Lambda}{\kappa^2}g_{\mu\nu}$ in the form of @exm-stress-fluid and find $\rho$ and $p$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Comparing $(\rho + p)u_\mu u_\nu - pg_{\mu\nu}$ with $\tfrac{\Lambda}{\kappa^2}g_{\mu\nu}$ for every $u$ requires $\rho + p = 0$ and
$-p = \Lambda/\kappa^2$: $\rho = \Lambda/\kappa^2$ and $p = -\rho$, the equation of state $w = -1$. The stress tensor is
the same in every frame, as the energy of empty space must be.
:::

The observed value of $\Lambda$ is tiny in natural units. The second exercise converts it to an energy density and
compares it with the Planck scale.

::: {#exr-gr-lambda-value}
#### The observed cosmological constant

With $\Lambda = 1.1 \times 10^{-52}\,\mathrm{m^{-2}}$, compute $\rho_\Lambda c^2 = \Lambda c^4/(8\pi G)$ in $\mathrm{J/m^3}$ and
in $\mathrm{eV^4}$ (using $\hbar c = 1.973 \times 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{eV\,m}$), and compare with the fourth power of the reduced
Planck mass $2.4 \times 10^{27}\,$eV.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\rho_\Lambda c^2 = 5.3 \times 10^{-10}\,\mathrm{J/m^3} = (2.3 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{eV})^4$, about $7 \times 10^{-121}$ of the Planck
density: the cosmological constant problem, the mismatch between this value and any natural estimate of the vacuum
energy.

{{< sage exr-gr-lambda-value >}}
:::

The cosmological constant modifies the Newtonian limit as well. The third exercise finds the extra force it
produces on a test particle near a point mass.

::: {#exr-gr-lambda-newtonian}
#### A repulsive force

Show that with a cosmological constant the trace-reversed equations read $R_{\mu\nu} = \kappa^2(T_{\mu\nu} - \tfrac12Tg_{\mu\nu}) -
\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}$ in four dimensions, deduce $\nabla^2\Phi = 4\pi G\rho - \Lambda$, and find the potential of a point
mass.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The trace of $G_{\mu\nu} - \Lambda g_{\mu\nu} = \kappa^2T_{\mu\nu}$ gives $R = -\kappa^2T - 4\Lambda$, and then $R_{\mu\nu} =
\kappa^2T_{\mu\nu} + \Lambda g_{\mu\nu} + \tfrac12Rg_{\mu\nu}$ is the stated form. Its $tt$ component in the weak field is
$\nabla^2\Phi = 4\pi G\rho - \Lambda$, solved outside a point mass by $\Phi = -GM/r - \Lambda r^2/6$: an attraction
plus a repulsion $\Lambda r/3$ growing with distance. Indeed $g_{tt} = 1 + 2\Phi = 1 - 2GM/r - \Lambda r^2/3$ is the
exact solution of @exr-gr-schwarzschild-de-sitter.
:::
::::

Without matter the Einstein equations still have many solutions, and those of highest symmetry serve as vacua. The
definition records the vacuum equations in their trace-reversed form, which says that the metric is an Einstein
metric.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-vacuum-solution}
#### Vacuum solution

A **vacuum solution** of the Einstein equations has $T_{\mu\nu} = 0$: $G_{\mu\nu} - \Lambda g_{\mu\nu} = 0$, equivalently
$R_{\mu\nu} = -\tfrac{2\Lambda}{n - 2}g_{\mu\nu}$ in $n$ dimensions (the sign is that of our signature, in which
$g_{tt} > 0$), so that a vacuum solution is an Einstein metric
(@def-einstein-metric). The maximally symmetric vacuum solutions are Minkowski space ($\Lambda = 0$), de Sitter
space ($\Lambda > 0$) and anti-de Sitter space ($\Lambda < 0$) [@carroll1997, p. 235].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
De Sitter space is the vacuum with positive cosmological constant. Its curvature is computed in three and in four
dimensions.

::: {#exm-vacuum-de-sitter}
#### De Sitter space

In three dimensions, with the Christoffel symbols $\Gamma^t_{xx} = \Gamma^t_{yy} = He^{2Ht}$, $\Gamma^x_{tx} =
\Gamma^y_{ty} = H$ (all others zero) one computes, as in @sec-ricci, $R_{\mu\nu} = -2H^2g_{\mu\nu}$ and $R = -6H^2$, hence
$G_{\mu\nu} - H^2g_{\mu\nu} = 0$: de Sitter space is the vacuum solution with $\Lambda = H^2$ (@prp-de-sitter). In
four dimensions, $R_{\mu\nu} = -3H^2g_{\mu\nu}$, $R = -12H^2$ and $\Lambda = 3H^2$ (@exr-de-sitter-4d): the Hubble rate of
the expansion is set by the cosmological constant.
:::

The three- and four-dimensional cases are instances of a single formula. The next example gives it in any dimension
$n$ for a metric of constant curvature.

::: {#exm-vacuum-einstein-n}
#### Einstein metrics in $n$ dimensions

For $R_{\mu\nu} = -(n - 1)H^2g_{\mu\nu}$ one has $R = -n(n - 1)H^2$ and $G_{\mu\nu} = \tfrac12(n - 1)(n - 2)H^2g_{\mu\nu}$:
for $n = 3$, $G_{\mu\nu} = H^2g_{\mu\nu}$, and for $n = 4$, $G_{\mu\nu} = 3H^2g_{\mu\nu}$, in agreement with the two
computations of @exm-vacuum-de-sitter.
:::

The same equations with the opposite sign of the curvature describe internal spheres. This is the mechanism behind
the compactifications of the last part.

::: {#exm-vacuum-sphere-internal}
#### A sphere as internal space

In Part VI the internal sphere of a compactification is an Einstein space with $R_{mn} = (n - 1)R_0^{-2}\gamma_{mn}$
for the positive-definite round metric $\gamma_{mn}$ (@exm-einstein-spheres), that is $R_{mn} = -(n - 1)R_0^{-2}g_{mn}$
for the internal metric $g_{mn} = -\gamma_{mn}$ of our signature, and the Einstein equations relate its radius $R_0$
to the flux or cosmological constant
that supports it (the Freund-Rubin mechanism): the same computation as for de Sitter space with the sign of the
curvature reversed.
:::

Anti-de Sitter space, met in @exr-gr-anti-de-sitter in the Poincaré coordinates, is also a hyperboloid, in a flat space
with two times. The next example gives its global coordinates, which show its unusual causal structure.

::: {#exm-grb-ads-global}
#### Global anti-de Sitter space

Four-dimensional anti-de Sitter space of unit radius is the quadric $U^2 + V^2 - X^2 - Y^2 - Z^2 = 1$ in the flat space with metric
$dU^2 + dV^2 - dX^2 - dY^2 - dZ^2$. With $U = \cosh\lambda\cos\alpha$, $V = \cosh\lambda\sin\alpha$ and $(X, Y, Z) = \sinh\lambda\,\hat n$,
$$
ds^2 = \cosh^2\lambda\,d\alpha^2 - d\lambda^2 - \sinh^2\lambda\,d\Omega^2 .
$$
The time $\alpha$ is periodic, so the quadric has closed timelike curves, and one passes to its universal cover, $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. A
radial light ray has $d\lambda = \cosh\lambda\,d\alpha$, so $\alpha = 2\arctan(\tanh(\lambda/2))$: it reaches $\lambda = \infty$ after the finite
time $\alpha = \pi/2$. The boundary at infinity is at a finite distance for light, the property on which the AdS/CFT
correspondence is built [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 2.86].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
