:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The vacuum equations fix the scalar curvature in terms of $\Lambda$. The first exercise works this out in four
dimensions.

::: {#exr-gr-vacuum-trace}
#### The curvature of a vacuum

Show that a four-dimensional vacuum solution has $R = -4\Lambda$ and $R_{\mu\nu} = -\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}$, and check these for
de Sitter space with $\Lambda = 3H^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The trace of $R_{\mu\nu} - \tfrac12Rg_{\mu\nu} = \Lambda g_{\mu\nu}$ is $-R = 4\Lambda$; substituting back, $R_{\mu\nu} = \Lambda g_{\mu\nu} +
\tfrac12Rg_{\mu\nu} = -\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}$, the case $n = 4$ of @def-vacuum-solution. For de Sitter space $R = -12H^2 =
-4\Lambda$ and $R_{\mu\nu} = -3H^2g_{\mu\nu}$, in agreement (@exr-de-sitter-4d).
:::

Anti-de Sitter space is the vacuum with negative cosmological constant. The second exercise computes its curvature
in Poincaré coordinates with SageManifolds.

::: {#exr-gr-anti-de-sitter}
#### Anti-de Sitter space

Show that $ds^2 = \tfrac{\ell^2}{z^2}(dt^2 - dx^2 - dy^2 - dz^2)$ on $z > 0$ has $R_{\mu\nu} = \tfrac{3}{\ell^2}g_{\mu\nu}$ and solves
the vacuum equations with $\Lambda = -3/\ell^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The metric is conformally flat, and SageManifolds gives $R_{\mu\nu} = 3\ell^{-2}g_{\mu\nu}$, $R = 12/\ell^2$. By
@exr-gr-vacuum-trace, $R_{\mu\nu} = -\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}$ with $\Lambda = -3/\ell^2 < 0$: the curvature has the opposite sign to
de Sitter space, as for the hyperbolic plane compared with the sphere.

{{< sage exr-gr-anti-de-sitter >}}
:::

Vacuum solutions need not be maximally symmetric. The third exercise checks a black hole in a universe with a
cosmological constant, combining this section with @sec-schwarzschild-flrw.

::: {#exr-gr-schwarzschild-de-sitter}
#### Schwarzschild-de Sitter

Show that $ds^2 = f\,dt^2 - f^{-1}dr^2 - r^2d\Omega^2$ with $f = 1 - 2m/r - \Lambda r^2/3$ satisfies $R_{\mu\nu} = -\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
SageManifolds gives $R_{\mu\nu} + \Lambda g_{\mu\nu} = 0$ and $R = -4\Lambda$. For $\Lambda = 0$ this is the Schwarzschild metric of
@def-gr-schwarzschild-metric, for $m = 0$ the static patch of de Sitter space (@exr-gr-int-de-sitter-three-ways); the
weak-field reading of $f$ is the potential of @exr-gr-lambda-newtonian.

{{< sage exr-gr-schwarzschild-de-sitter >}}
:::

The embedding of the previous example makes the light rays of anti-de Sitter space simple. The next exercise shows
that they are straight lines of the flat ambient space, by a Lagrange multiplier argument.

::: {#exr-grb-ads-null}
#### Light rays are straight lines

Show that the geodesics of the quadric $X\cdot X = 1$ of @exm-grb-ads-global, with $X\cdot Y = \eta_{ab}X^aY^b$ the ambient metric, are the
extremals of $\int\bigl(\tfrac12\dot X\cdot\dot X + \lambda(X\cdot X - 1)\bigr)d\sigma$, that $\dot X\cdot\dot X$ is constant along them, and that the null ones obey
$\ddot X^a = 0$: they are straight lines $X = A + \sigma B$ with $A\cdot A = 1$, $A\cdot B = 0$, $B\cdot B = 0$
[@blennow2022relativity, Problem 2.86].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The multiplier enforces the constraint, and the extremals of the constrained energy functional are the geodesics of the
induced metric. The Euler-Lagrange equation is $\ddot X^a = 2\lambda X^a$. Differentiating $X\cdot X = 1$ twice gives $X\cdot\dot X = 0$ and $\dot X\cdot\dot X +
X\cdot\ddot X = 0$, so $2\lambda = -\dot X\cdot\dot X$; and $\tfrac{d}{d\sigma}(\dot X\cdot\dot X) = 2\dot X\cdot\ddot X = 4\lambda X\cdot\dot X = 0$. For a null geodesic $\dot X\cdot\dot X = 0$,
hence $\lambda = 0$ and $\ddot X = 0$. The line $A + \sigma B$ stays on the quadric for all $\sigma$ iff $A\cdot A = 1$, $A\cdot B = 0$ and $B\cdot B = 0$. Timelike
geodesics, with $\dot X\cdot\dot X = 1$, obey $\ddot X = -X$ instead: they are ellipses $A\cos\sigma + B\sin\sigma$, all returning to their starting
point after $\sigma = 2\pi$, which is why anti-de Sitter space acts like a box for massive particles.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

In two dimensions the Einstein tensor vanishes because the Ricci tensor and half the scalar curvature times the metric
cancel exactly. The proposition states this on the unit sphere, and @exr-einstein-2d proves it for every metric.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-einstein-2d}
#### The Einstein tensor vanishes in two dimensions

On the unit sphere $R_{ij} - \tfrac12R\,g_{ij} = 0$ on the chart domain. The same holds for an arbitrary
two-dimensional metric (@exr-einstein-2d).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** `KaluzaKlein.Relativity.sphere_einstein_zero`.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Relativity.sphere_einstein_zero >}}


**Sage.** The statement for an arbitrary two-dimensional metric is checked by exact computation with SageManifolds in
the solution of @exr-einstein-2d.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A flat two-dimensional metric satisfies the proposition trivially, since every curvature tensor vanishes. The flat torus
is the compact example in two dimensions.

::: {#exm-gr-2d-torus}
#### The flat torus

On the flat torus of @exm-riemann-torus all curvature vanishes, $R_{ij} = 0$ and $R = 0$, so $G_{ij} = 0$ without any
cancellation; the Gauss-Bonnet integral is $4\pi\chi = 0$ (@exr-eh-topological).
:::

The interesting cases are curved metrics, where $R_{ij}$ and $\tfrac12Rg_{ij}$ are both non-zero and cancel. The radius
of a sphere shows that the vacuum equations cannot even fix the size of a two-dimensional space.

::: {#exm-gr-2d-sphere-radius}
#### A sphere of any radius

For the round sphere of radius $a$, $R_{ij} = a^{-2}g_{ij}$ and $R = 2/a^2$ (@exm-sphere-curvature-radius), so $G_{ij} =
a^{-2}g_{ij} - a^{-2}g_{ij} = 0$ for every $a$: no equation selects the radius.
:::

Two-dimensional de Sitter space, drawn in @fig-de-sitter, is a Lorentzian example. It is curved but has zero
Einstein tensor, as computed in @exr-gr-2d-ds2.

::: {#exm-gr-2d-ds2}
#### Two-dimensional de Sitter space

$ds^2 = dt^2 - e^{2Ht}dx^2$ has $R_{\mu\nu} = -H^2g_{\mu\nu}$ and $R = -2H^2$, the case $n = 2$ of
@exm-vacuum-einstein-n, whose formula $G_{\mu\nu} = \tfrac12(n - 1)(n - 2)H^2g_{\mu\nu}$ indeed vanishes at $n = 2$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks the Lorentzian example with SageManifolds. It confirms the values of the Ricci tensor and
the scalar curvature quoted in the last example.

::: {#exr-gr-2d-ds2}
#### De Sitter space in two dimensions

Compute the Ricci tensor, the scalar curvature and the Einstein tensor of $ds^2 = dt^2 - e^{2Ht}dx^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The only non-zero Christoffel symbols are $\Gamma^t_{xx} = He^{2Ht}$ and $\Gamma^x_{tx} = H$; the Ricci tensor is $-H^2g$, the
scalar curvature $-2H^2$ and the Einstein tensor zero.

{{< sage exr-gr-2d-ds2 >}}
:::

The second exercise, from the old version of this section, proves the statement for every two-dimensional metric.
Its solution uses the single independent component of the Riemann tensor and computes a generic metric explicitly.

::: {#exr-einstein-2d}
#### Two dimensions

Show that the Einstein tensor of an arbitrary two-dimensional metric vanishes.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In two dimensions the Riemann tensor has one independent component and $R_{ijkl} = \tfrac12R(g_{ik}g_{jl} -
g_{il}g_{jk})$ (@sec-riemann); contracting, $R_{jl} = \tfrac12R\,g_{jl}$, so $G_{jl} = 0$. In Sage, for a generic
symmetric metric with three arbitrary functions, built as a SageManifolds metric:

{{< sage exr-einstein-2d >}}

:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** The sphere case is `KaluzaKlein.Relativity.sphere_einstein_zero` of @prp-einstein-2d.

**Sage.** The generic metric is checked by exact computation with SageManifolds in the solution.
:::

Three dimensions are the next special case: there the Einstein equations have content, but no gravitational waves.
The third exercise explains why by counting components.

::: {#exr-gr-3d-flat}
#### Three-dimensional gravity

Show that in three dimensions the Riemann tensor has as many independent components as the Ricci tensor, and deduce
that every solution of the vacuum equations with $\Lambda = 0$ is flat.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The Riemann tensor has $n^2(n^2 - 1)/12 = 6$ components for $n = 3$, and the symmetric Ricci tensor has $n(n + 1)/2 =
6$. In fact $R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}$ is a linear combination of $R_{\mu\rho}g_{\nu\sigma}$-type terms and $Rg_{\mu\rho}g_{\nu\sigma}$-type
terms. In vacuum with $\Lambda = 0$, $R_{\mu\nu} = 0$ (@exr-gr-trace-reversed), hence $R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma} = 0$: the metric is flat
locally, and gravity in three dimensions has no local degrees of freedom. Massive objects only produce a conical
deficit angle.
:::
::::

De Sitter space in three dimensions is small enough to be computed completely, from the metric to the field
equation. The proposition records the inverse metric, the connection, the curvature and the vacuum equation.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-de-sitter}
#### Curvature of three-dimensional de Sitter space

For $ds^2 = dt^2 - e^{2Ht}(dx^2 + dy^2)$: the inverse metric is $\operatorname{diag}(1, -e^{-2Ht}, -e^{-2Ht})$, the
Christoffel symbols are as stated in @exm-vacuum-de-sitter, $R_{\mu\nu} = -2H^2g_{\mu\nu}$, $R = -6H^2$ and $G_{\mu\nu} -
H^2g_{\mu\nu} = 0$, everywhere, since $e^{2Ht} \neq 0$.
:::

**Lean.** `KaluzaKlein.Relativity.dS3_invMetric`, `KaluzaKlein.Relativity.dS3_christoffel_fun`,
`KaluzaKlein.Relativity.dS3_ricci_eq`, `KaluzaKlein.Relativity.dS3_scalarCurvature` and
`KaluzaKlein.Relativity.dS3_einstein`, without any chart hypothesis.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.Relativity.dS3_einstein >}}


**Sage.** The embedding as a hyperboloid is checked in Sage (`figures/de_sitter.sage`).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The coordinate $t$ of de Sitter space is the proper time of the comoving observers. Their separation grows
exponentially at a constant rate.

::: {#exm-gr-ds-hubble}
#### A constant Hubble rate

Two comoving observers at fixed $x$ and $x + \Delta x$ are at physical distance $d = e^{Ht}\Delta x$ at time $t$, so $\dot d
= Hd$: they recede at a speed proportional to their distance, with the constant Hubble rate $H = \dot a/a$ and
$a = e^{Ht}$ (@def-gr-flrw-metric).
:::

Exponential expansion hides part of the universe from every observer. The light rays of the flat slicing make this
explicit.

::: {#exm-gr-ds-horizon}
#### The cosmological horizon

A light ray $dx/dt = e^{-Ht}$ sent at time $t$ from $x = 0$ reaches at most the comoving coordinate $\int_t^\infty
e^{-Ht'}dt' = e^{-Ht}/H$, the physical distance $1/H$. Events farther away than $1/H$ can never be influenced by the
observer: de Sitter space has a horizon, which in static coordinates is the surface $r = 1/H$ of
@exr-gr-int-de-sitter-three-ways.
:::

The flat slicing covers only half of de Sitter space. The full space is the hyperboloid of @fig-de-sitter, on which
the symmetry is manifest.

![Two-dimensional de Sitter space as the hyperboloid $X_0^2 - X_1^2 - X_2^2 = -1/H^2$ in three-dimensional
Minkowski space, with the flat-slicing coordinates: surfaces of constant $t$ (red circles, growing like $e^{Ht}$)
and lines of constant $x$ (blue). The induced metric is $dt^2 - e^{2Ht}dx^2$. Generated by
`figures/de_sitter.sage`.](figures/de_sitter.png){#fig-de-sitter width=55%}

::: {#exm-gr-ds-hyperboloid}
#### The hyperboloid

$n$-dimensional de Sitter space is the hyperboloid $X_0^2 - X_1^2 - \dots - X_n^2 = -1/H^2$ in $(n + 1)$-dimensional
Minkowski space, and the Lorentz group $SO(1, n)$ of the ambient space acts on it by isometries: dimension $n(n + 1)/2$,
the maximum (@def-maximally-symmetric). The flat slicing covers the half $X_0 + X_n > 0$, as @fig-de-sitter shows for
$n = 2$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** The case $n = 2$ is computed in Sage (`figures/de_sitter.sage`).
:::

In the flat slicing the geodesics of de Sitter space are simple too. The next example shows that free particles and
light move on straight lines of the comoving coordinates, the expansion acting only on the speed.

::: {#exm-grb-ds-straight}
#### Straight comoving paths

For $ds^2 = dt^2 - e^{2t/R}(dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2)$ the metric does not depend on $\vec x$, so $e^{2t/R}\,d\vec x/d\tau = \vec p$ is constant along
a geodesic. The direction of $d\vec x/d\tau$ is fixed: free particles and photons move on straight lines in the comoving
coordinates. A photon sent from $x = X$ towards the origin at $t = 0$ has $dx/dt = -e^{-t/R}$ and arrives at $t = -R\ln(1 - X/R)$ if
$X < R$, never if $X \geq R$, the horizon of @exm-gr-ds-horizon [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 2.83].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Global coordinates on the hyperboloid show the same horizon from another angle. The next example follows light on the
two-dimensional de Sitter space, where the whole spacetime can be drawn.

::: {#exm-grb-ds2-global}
#### Light on the two-dimensional hyperboloid

On $x_0^2 - x_1^2 - x_2^2 = -1$ in three-dimensional Minkowski space, $x_0 = \sinh\tau$, $x_1 = \cosh\tau\cos\phi$, $x_2 = \cosh\tau\sin\phi$ give
$ds^2 = d\tau^2 - \cosh^2\tau\,d\phi^2$. A light ray has $d\phi = d\tau/\cosh\tau$, so $\phi(\tau) - \phi(\tau_0) = \operatorname{gd}\tau - \operatorname{gd}\tau_0$ with the
Gudermannian $\operatorname{gd}\tau = 2\arctan(\tanh(\tau/2))$, which runs from $-\pi/2$ to $\pi/2$. Over the whole history of the universe a
ray covers half the circle; sent at $x_0 = 0$ from $\phi = 0$ it reaches $\phi = \pi/2$ only as $x_0 \to \infty$, and the antipodal half
of the circle never receives it [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 2.79].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise, from the old version of this section, extends the computation of @prp-de-sitter to four dimensions.
It gives the value $\Lambda = 3H^2$ used in cosmology.

::: {#exr-de-sitter-4d}
#### Four-dimensional de Sitter space

Compute the Ricci tensor and scalar curvature of $ds^2 = dt^2 - e^{2Ht}d\vec x^2$ in four dimensions and find
$\Lambda$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The non-zero symbols are $\Gamma^t_{ij} = He^{2Ht}\delta_{ij}$ and $\Gamma^i_{tj} = H\delta^i_j$; the Ricci tensor is
$-3H^2g_{\mu\nu}$, $R = -12H^2$, $G_{\mu\nu} = 3H^2g_{\mu\nu}$ and $\Lambda = 3H^2$. In Sage:

{{< sage exr-de-sitter-4d >}}
:::

Geodesics of de Sitter space other than the comoving ones slow down. The second exercise shows that the momentum of
a free particle decays like $1/a$.

::: {#exr-gr-ds-peculiar}
#### Peculiar velocities decay

For a geodesic of $ds^2 = dt^2 - a(t)^2d\vec x^2$, show that $a^2\,dx^i/d\tau$ is constant, using that $g$ does not depend on
$x^i$. Deduce that the momentum measured by comoving observers, $p = ma\,|d\vec x/d\tau|$, decreases as $1/a$; what does this
mean for de Sitter space?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\partial_i$ is a Killing vector, so $g(\partial_i, u) = -a^2\,dx^i/d\tau$ is conserved along geodesics (as for $E$ in
@exr-gr-nl-energy). Hence $a\,|d\vec x/d\tau| \propto 1/a$ and $p \propto 1/a$. In de Sitter space $a = e^{Ht}$, so any
initial motion relative to the comoving observers dies away exponentially, and the comoving geodesics of
@exm-equivalence-geodesics are attractors. For light the same law is the cosmological redshift (@exr-gr-flrw-redshift).
:::

Translations in time are not obviously symmetries of the flat slicing, because the metric depends on $t$. The third
exercise finds the Killing vector that combines a time translation with a dilation.

::: {#exr-gr-ds-killing}
#### A hidden time translation

Show that $\xi = \partial_t - H(x\partial_x + y\partial_y + z\partial_z)$ is a Killing vector of four-dimensional de Sitter space in
flat slicing (@def-killing), while $\partial_t$ is not.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The finite transformation $t \mapsto t + c$, $\vec x \mapsto e^{-Hc}\vec x$ maps $e^{2Ht}d\vec x^2$ to $e^{2H(t + c)}e^{-2Hc}d\vec x^2$,
an isometry; $\xi$ is its generator. SageManifolds gives $\mathcal{L}_\xi g = 0$ and $\mathcal{L}_{\partial_t}g = -2He^{2Ht}d\vec x^2 \neq
0$.

{{< sage exr-gr-ds-killing >}}
:::

Redshifts between comoving observers measure the expansion. The next exercise computes the redshift in two-dimensional
de Sitter space exactly, including the horizon beyond which no signal arrives.

::: {#exr-grb-ds2-redshift}
#### Redshift in de Sitter space

In $ds^2 = dt^2 - e^{2t/R}dx^2$ a comoving observer at $x_0$ emits light at time $t_e$ towards a comoving observer at $x_1 = x_0 + d$. With
Sage, find the arrival time and show that $1 + z = \bigl(1 - de^{t_e/R}/R\bigr)^{-1}$. What happens when $de^{t_e/R} \geq R$, and what is
$z$ for small $d$? [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 2.139]
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Along the ray $dx/dt = e^{-t/R}$, and the frequency scales as $1/a$ (@exr-gr-flrw-redshift):

{{< sage exr-grb-ds2-redshift >}}

For $de^{t_e/R} \geq R$ the light never arrives: the receiver is beyond the horizon of the emission event. For small $d$, $z =
He^{t_e/R}d$ with $H = 1/R$, Hubble's law with the proper distance $e^{t_e/R}d$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A field on de Sitter space feels the expansion as friction. The next exercise computes the wave operator and finds its
simplest solutions, which show the damping explicitly.

::: {#exr-grb-ds2-wave}
#### Waves on two-dimensional de Sitter space

With Sage, compute $\Box\Phi = g^{\mu\nu}\nabla_\mu\nabla_\nu\Phi$ for $ds^2 = dt^2 - e^{2t/R}dx^2$. Find the solutions that do not depend on $x$, and
show that $e^{ik(x - \eta)}$ with the conformal time $\eta = -Re^{-t/R}$ is a solution. [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 2.140]
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
SageManifolds gives the operator, and the two families of solutions are checked by substitution:

{{< sage exr-grb-ds2-wave >}}

The term $\Phi_t/R = H\Phi_t$ is Hubble friction: homogeneous solutions settle to a constant, $A + Be^{-t/R}$. In conformal time
$ds^2 = e^{2t/R}(d\eta^2 - dx^2)$ is conformally flat, and in two dimensions $\sqrt{|g|}g^{\mu\nu}$ is conformally invariant, so the
massless wave equation is the flat one, $\partial_\eta^2\Phi - \partial_x^2\Phi = 0$.
:::

## Black holes and cosmology {#sec-schwarzschild-flrw}

The Einstein equations are non-linear, and exact solutions exist only under strong symmetry assumptions. Two of them
carry most of the observable content of the theory. Outside a spherically symmetric mass the solution is unique, the
Schwarzschild metric; it contains a horizon, describes black holes, and its geodesics give the perihelion advance of
Mercury and the bending of light. A homogeneous and isotropic universe is described by the FLRW metric, whose single
function $a(t)$ obeys the Friedmann equations. In this section we keep $G$ explicit in the definitions and set $G = c
= 1$ in computations, writing $m = GM$ for the mass in units of length.

### The Schwarzschild solution

The simplest source of gravity is a single spherical body, and the simplest region to study is the empty space
around it. There the vacuum equations $R_{\mu\nu} = 0$ must hold, and spherical symmetry reduces them to ordinary
differential equations whose solution was found by Schwarzschild in 1916.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-gr-schwarzschild-metric}
#### Schwarzschild metric

The **Schwarzschild metric** of mass $M > 0$ is
$$
ds^2 = \Bigl(1 - \frac{2GM}{r}\Bigr)dt^2 - \Bigl(1 - \frac{2GM}{r}\Bigr)^{-1}dr^2 - r^2\bigl(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2\bigr),
$$ {#eq-gr-schwarzschild}
on $r > 2GM$, where $r$ is defined by the area $4\pi r^2$ of the spheres of constant $t$ and $r$. It is a vacuum solution,
$R_{\mu\nu} = 0$ (@prp-gr-schwarzschild), and by **Birkhoff's theorem** it is the only spherically symmetric one: the
gravitational field outside any spherical body is @eq-gr-schwarzschild [@carroll1997, ch. 7, with the overall sign of
our signature]. The radius $r_s = 2GM$ is the **Schwarzschild radius**.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Far from the mass the metric must reduce to the weak field of @def-newtonian-limit. The time component does so
directly.

::: {#exm-gr-schw-newtonian}
#### The Newtonian potential

At large $r$, $g_{tt} = 1 - 2GM/r = 1 + 2\Phi$ with $\Phi = -GM/r$, the Newtonian potential of a point mass
(@exm-newtonian-point-mass). The radial component $g_{rr} = -(1 + 2GM/r + \dots)$ differs from the $-(1 - 2\Phi)$ of
@prp-newtonian-limit only by the choice of radial coordinate, as @exr-gr-schw-isotropic shows.
:::

The Schwarzschild radius is small for ordinary bodies. Comparing it with their actual radii shows why the horizon plays
no role in the solar system.

::: {#exm-gr-schw-radius}
#### Schwarzschild radii

With $GM_\odot/c^2 = 1.48\,$km, the Sun has $r_s = 2.95\,$km, far inside its radius of $696\,000\,$km where the vacuum
solution does not apply; the Earth has $r_s = 8.9\,$mm. Only bodies compressed below $r_s$, black holes, have the
surface $r = 2GM$ outside them.
:::

Birkhoff's theorem has a striking consequence for dynamics. Whatever a spherical star does internally, its exterior
gravitational field cannot change at all.

::: {#exm-gr-schw-birkhoff}
#### No spherical waves

A spherically symmetric star that pulsates or collapses keeps the exterior metric @eq-gr-schwarzschild with constant $M$:
there is no spherically symmetric gravitational radiation, just as there is no monopole electromagnetic radiation.
Gravitational waves need a changing quadrupole moment.
:::

The Schwarzschild metric is curved, yet it can be drawn as a surface in a flat space of higher dimension. The next
example gives Fronsdal's embedding into six-dimensional Minkowski space.

::: {#exm-grb-fronsdal}
#### An embedding in six dimensions

With $r_s = 2GM$, set $Z_1 = 2r_s\sinh\frac{t}{2r_s}f(r)$, $Z_2 = 2r_s\cosh\frac{t}{2r_s}f(r)$, $Z_3 = g(r)$ and $(Z_4, Z_5, Z_6) = r\,\hat n(\theta, \phi)$
in the space with metric $dZ_1^2 - dZ_2^2 - \dots - dZ_6^2$. Then $dZ_1^2 - dZ_2^2 = f^2dt^2 - 4r_s^2f'^2dr^2$, and @eq-gr-schwarzschild is reproduced
by $f = \sqrt{1 - r_s/r}$ and
$$
g'(r)^2 = \frac{r_s}{r}\Bigl(1 + \frac{r_s}{r} + \frac{r_s^2}{r^2}\Bigr),
$$
since then $4r_s^2f'^2 + g'^2 + 1 = (1 - r_s/r)^{-1}$. The embedding is regular at $r = r_s$, where $f = 0$: the horizon is the
intersection with $Z_1 = \pm Z_2$, a first sign that it is not a singularity [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 2.77].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

**Lean.** Pending.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The size of a black hole of given mass follows from the definition. The first exercise computes a few, from stellar
to galactic masses.

::: {#exr-gr-schw-radius-numbers}
#### Black holes of different masses

Compute $r_s = 2GM/c^2$ for a black hole of $10$ solar masses and for Sagittarius A$^*$, the black hole at the centre of
the Galaxy, of $4.3 \times 10^6$ solar masses, and compare the latter with the radius of the Earth's orbit, $1.5 \times
10^8\,$km. What is the mean density inside $r_s$, as a function of $M$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$r_s = 2.95\,$km per solar mass: $29.5\,$km and $1.27 \times 10^7\,$km, about $0.085$ of the Earth-Sun distance. The mean
density $M/(\tfrac43\pi r_s^3) = 3c^6/(32\pi G^3M^2)$ decreases as $M^{-2}$: a stellar black hole is denser than a nucleus,
while one of $10^8$ solar masses has the density of water.
:::

That $R_{\mu\nu} = 0$ does not mean that space is flat: the Riemann tensor carries the tidal field. The second
exercise computes one component with SageManifolds.

::: {#exr-gr-schw-ricci-flat}
#### Ricci flat but curved

Compute the Ricci tensor of @eq-gr-schwarzschild (with $G = 1$, $m = M$) and the component $R^r{}_{trt}$ of the Riemann
tensor, and compare the latter with the radial tidal acceleration of @exr-gr-tidal.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$R_{\mu\nu} = 0$ and $R = 0$, but $R^r{}_{trt} = -2m(r - 2m)/r^4 = -\tfrac{2m}{r^3}(1 - 2m/r)$. For a particle momentarily at
rest, $u^t = (1 - 2m/r)^{-1/2}$, and geodesic deviation in the radial direction gives $\ddot\xi^r = R^r{}_{ttr}(u^t)^2\xi^r = -
R^r{}_{trt}(u^t)^2\xi^r = \tfrac{2m}{r^3}\xi^r$: the radial stretching $2GM/r^3$ of @exr-gr-tidal.

{{< sage exr-gr-schw-ricci-flat >}}
:::

Different radial coordinates can make the metric look different. The third exercise finds isotropic coordinates, in
which the spatial part is conformally flat and the weak-field form of @def-newtonian-limit appears exactly.

::: {#exr-gr-schw-isotropic}
#### Isotropic coordinates

Substitute $r = \rho(1 + m/2\rho)^2$ in @eq-gr-schwarzschild and show that the metric becomes $\bigl(\tfrac{1 - m/2\rho}{1 +
m/2\rho}\bigr)^2dt^2 - (1 + m/2\rho)^4(d\rho^2 + \rho^2d\Omega^2)$. Expand to first order in $m$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$1 - 2m/r = \bigl(\tfrac{1 - m/2\rho}{1 + m/2\rho}\bigr)^2$, $dr/d\rho = (1 - m/2\rho)(1 + m/2\rho)$, so $g_{\rho\rho} = -(1 + m/2\rho)^4$, and
$r^2 = \rho^2(1 + m/2\rho)^4$ gives the same factor on the sphere. To first order: $g_{tt} = 1 - 2m/\rho$ and $g_{ij} = -(1 +
2m/\rho)\delta_{ij}$, which is exactly the weak-field metric of @prp-newtonian-limit with $\Phi = -m/\rho$.

{{< sage exr-gr-schw-isotropic >}}
:::

The Kretschmann scalar of @prp-gr-schwarzschild is finite at $r = 2m$, but a single invariant can hide divergent
components. The next exercise computes all the curvature components that an observer measures, which are the tidal
accelerations.

::: {#exr-grb-frame-curvature}
#### Curvature in the observer's frame

With Sage, compute the components $R_{(abab)}$ of the Riemann tensor of @eq-gr-schwarzschild ($G = 1$, $m = M$) in the orthonormal frame
$e_{(t)} = (1 - 2m/r)^{-1/2}\partial_t$, $e_{(r)} = (1 - 2m/r)^{1/2}\partial_r$, $e_{(\theta)} = r^{-1}\partial_\theta$, $e_{(\phi)} = (r\sin\theta)^{-1}\partial_\phi$, and check
the Kretschmann scalar. Are they finite at $r = 2m$? What do they mean for a falling body?
[@plebanski2024introduction, Sec. 14.17, Exercise 7; @blennow2022relativity, Problem 2.110]
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Dividing the coordinate components by the norms of the coordinate vectors:

{{< sage exr-grb-frame-curvature >}}

All components are $\pm2m/r^3$ or $\pm m/r^3$, finite at $r = 2m$ and divergent only at $r = 0$; the frame itself is singular at the
horizon, but the components in the frame of a radially falling observer are the same, since radial boosts leave these
components unchanged. By the geodesic deviation equation a body is stretched radially with tidal acceleration $2m/r^3$ per
unit length and compressed sideways with $m/r^3$, as in Newtonian gravity (@exr-gr-tidal); at $r = 0$ the stretching becomes
infinite.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

The coefficient $g_{rr}$ blows up at $r = 2GM$. This is not a singularity of spacetime but of the coordinates, and the
surface $r = 2GM$ has a physical meaning of its own: nothing that crosses it inwards can come back.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-gr-event-horizon}
#### Event horizon

The **event horizon** of the Schwarzschild spacetime is the surface $r = 2GM$. In the ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein
coordinate $v = t + r_*$, with the tortoise coordinate $r_* = r + 2GM\log|r/2GM - 1|$, the metric reads
$$
ds^2 = \Bigl(1 - \frac{2GM}{r}\Bigr)dv^2 - 2\,dv\,dr - r^2d\Omega^2,
$$ {#eq-gr-eddington-finkelstein}
which is regular at $r = 2GM$ and extends the spacetime to $0 < r < 2GM$. Inside the horizon every future-directed
timelike or null curve has decreasing $r$; the region $r < 2GM$ is a **black hole**, and its boundary is the boundary of
the set of events from which signals can reach infinity [@carroll1997, ch. 7]. The curvature singularity is at
$r = 0$, where $R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}R^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma} = 48G^2M^2/r^6$ diverges (@prp-gr-schwarzschild).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The light cones in the Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates show the horizon at work. They are drawn in the left panel
of @fig-schwarzschild.

::: {#exm-gr-horizon-cones}
#### Tilting light cones

In the coordinates $(r, \tilde t = v - r)$ radial light rays have slopes $d\tilde t/dr = -1$ (ingoing) and $(1 + 2m/r)/(1 -
2m/r)$ (outgoing). Outside the horizon the outgoing slope is positive; at $r = 2m$ it is infinite, the ray stays at
$r = 2m$; inside it is negative, so both rays move to smaller $r$. The cones tilt inwards as the horizon is crossed.
:::

In Schwarzschild coordinates the approach to the horizon takes forever. The tortoise coordinate measures how, and
makes the radial light rays straight.

::: {#exm-gr-horizon-tortoise}
#### The tortoise coordinate

Radial light rays obey $dt = \pm dr/(1 - 2m/r) = \pm dr_*$, and $r_* \to -\infty$ as $r \to 2m$: a light ray needs infinite
coordinate time $t$ to reach the horizon. Since $t$ is the time of a distant observer, the infall is never seen to
complete, although it takes finite proper time (@exr-gr-horizon-infall-time).
:::

The horizon is also a surface of infinite redshift. Static clocks near it run arbitrarily slowly compared with
clocks far away.

::: {#exm-gr-horizon-redshift}
#### Infinite redshift

A static source at radius $r$ emitting at frequency $\nu$ is received at infinity at $\nu_\infty = \nu\sqrt{1 - 2m/r}$
(@exm-newtonian-redshift, now exact). As $r \to 2m$ the ratio tends to zero: an object falling in appears to freeze and
fade at the horizon.
:::

Staying at a fixed radius near a black hole requires a rocket. The next example computes the acceleration that the
rocket must provide, which grows without bound at the horizon.

::: {#exm-grb-static-acceleration}
#### Hovering above a black hole

A static observer at radius $r$ has $u = (1 - 2m/r)^{-1/2}\partial_t$, and its four-acceleration $a^\mu = u^\nu\nabla_\nu u^\mu$ has the only component
$a^r = \Gamma^r_{tt}(u^t)^2 = m/r^2$, so the proper acceleration is
$$
\alpha = \sqrt{-g_{rr}}\,a^r = \frac{m}{r^2\sqrt{1 - 2m/r}} .
$$
For $r \gg m$ this is Newton's $GM/r^2$; it diverges at $r = 2m$, where no observer can stay at rest. The redshifted value
$\sqrt{1 - 2m/r}\,\alpha \to 1/(4m)$ is the surface gravity of @exr-gr-horizon-temperature [@blennow2022relativity, Problems 2.94 and 2.100].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Inside the horizon every observer reaches $r = 0$ in a finite proper time. The next example computes the longest
possible time, for a fall from rest.

::: {#exm-grb-max-proper-time}
#### The longest fall

Radial free fall from rest at $r_0$ has $E^2 = 1 - 2m/r_0$ and $\dot r^2 = 2m/r - 2m/r_0$, solved by the cycloid $r = \tfrac{r_0}{2}(1 + \cos\eta)$,
$\tau = \sqrt{r_0^3/8m}\,(\eta + \sin\eta)$: the singularity $\eta = \pi$ is reached after $\tau = \pi\sqrt{r_0^3/8m}$, the Newtonian free-fall time. From
the horizon, $r_0 = 2m$, this is $\tau = \pi m = \pi GM/c^3$, about $1.5 \times 10^{-4}\,$s for ten solar masses; any other motion inside
reaches $r = 0$ sooner, so firing a rocket only shortens the remaining time [@blennow2022relativity, Problems 2.91 and 2.96].
:::

**Lean.** Pending.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The Eddington-Finkelstein form follows from the Schwarzschild form by a change of coordinate. The first exercise
carries it out and identifies the ingoing light rays.

::: {#exr-gr-horizon-ef}
#### Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates

Show that $dr_*/dr = (1 - 2m/r)^{-1}$, substitute $dt = dv - dr/(1 - 2m/r)$ in @eq-gr-schwarzschild, and obtain
@eq-gr-eddington-finkelstein. Which curves are the ingoing light rays?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\tfrac{d}{dr}\bigl(r + 2m\log|r/2m - 1|\bigr) = 1 + \tfrac{2m}{r - 2m} = \tfrac{r}{r - 2m}$. With $f = 1 - 2m/r$, $f(dv - dr/f)^2 - dr^2/f =
f\,dv^2 - 2dv\,dr$: the $dr^2$ terms cancel, and the metric coefficients are smooth at $f = 0$. Ingoing radial light
rays are the lines $v = \text{constant}$, since then $ds^2 = 0$ with $d\Omega = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Exact computation (`figures/schwarzschild.sage`).
:::

A falling observer reaches the horizon and the centre in finite proper time. The second exercise computes it for a
fall from rest at infinity.

::: {#exr-gr-horizon-infall-time}
#### Falling in

For radial free fall from rest at infinity, $E = 1$ and $L = 0$, show that $(dr/d\tau)^2 = 2m/r$ and compute the proper
time from $r = 2m$ to $r = 0$. Show that the coordinate time $t$ diverges near $r = 2m$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The normalisation $g(u, u) = 1$ with $E = (1 - 2m/r)\dot t$ gives $\dot r^2 = E^2 - (1 - 2m/r) = 2m/r$, exactly the
Newtonian energy equation. Then $\tau = \int_0^{2m}\sqrt{r/2m}\,dr = 4m/3$: about $66\,\mu$s for a black hole of ten solar
masses. Near $r = 2m(1 + \epsilon)$, $|dt/dr| \approx 1/\epsilon + \tfrac32$, and with $dr = 2m\,d\epsilon$ the coordinate time grows like
$t \approx -2m\log\epsilon \to \infty$.

{{< sage exr-gr-horizon-infall-time >}}
:::

Black holes are not completely black once quantum mechanics is included. The third exercise quotes the result and
relates it to the redshift at the horizon.

::: {#exr-gr-horizon-temperature}
#### Surface gravity and temperature

The **surface gravity** $\kappa_s$ is the redshifted acceleration needed to hold a static observer at the horizon,
$\kappa_s = \tfrac12f'(r_s)$ for $f = 1 - 2m/r$. Compute it, and evaluate Hawking's temperature $T_H = \kappa_s/2\pi$ (in units
$\hbar = c = k_B = G = 1$, quoted, not derived here) for a black hole of one solar mass, using $T_H = 6.2 \times
10^{-8}\,\mathrm{K}\,(M_\odot/M)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$f'(r) = 2m/r^2$, so $\kappa_s = m/r_s^2 = 1/(4m)$ and $T_H = 1/(8\pi m)$: larger black holes are colder. For one solar mass
$T_H = 6.2 \times 10^{-8}\,$K, far below the $2.7\,$K of the cosmic microwave background, so astrophysical black holes
absorb more than they radiate.
:::

The Kruskal coordinates cover the interior as well as the exterior. The next exercise uses them to show that nothing
leaves the black-hole region, which is the content of the word horizon.

::: {#exr-grb-kruskal-trapped}
#### No way out

In the Kruskal-Szekeres coordinates $ds^2 = \tfrac{16m^2}{r}e^{(2m - r)/2m}\,du\,dv - r^2d\Omega^2$ with $uv = (2m - r)e^{(r - 2m)/2m}$ and
$t = 2m\ln(-v/u)$ outside, show that future-directed causal curves have $\dot u \geq 0$, $\dot v \geq 0$, that $uv$ is a decreasing function of $r$,
and conclude that a curve entering the region $u > 0$, $v > 0$ never returns to $r > 2m$ [@blennow2022relativity, Problems 2.107-2.108].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A causal curve has $\tfrac{16m^2}{r}e^{(2m - r)/2m}\dot u\dot v \geq r^2\dot\Omega^2 \geq 0$, so $\dot u$ and $\dot v$ have the same sign (or one vanishes); in the
exterior $u < 0 < v$, increasing $t$ at fixed $r$ means $-v/u$ increasing at fixed $uv$, that is $u$ and $v$ increasing, which fixes
the future direction everywhere by continuity. $\tfrac{d}{dr}\bigl[(2m - r)e^{(r - 2m)/2m}\bigr] = -\tfrac{r}{2m}e^{(r - 2m)/2m} < 0$. In the region $u, v > 0$,
$\tfrac{d}{d\sigma}(uv) = \dot uv + u\dot v \geq 0$, so $uv$ does not decrease and $r$ does not increase along the curve; since $r > 2m$ would need
$uv < 0$, the curve stays at $r < 2m$, and reaches $r = 0$ at $uv = 2m/e$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

The geometry of the solution and the motion in it fit in one proposition. It collects the exact statements on
curvature, light cones and geodesics, and the two classic effects, the perihelion advance and light deflection.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-gr-schwarzschild}
#### Geodesics of the Schwarzschild metric

With $G = 1$ and $m = M$: (a) @eq-gr-schwarzschild is Ricci flat and its Kretschmann scalar is
$R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}R^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma} = 48m^2/r^6$; (b) radial light rays have $dr/dt = \pm(1 - 2m/r)$, the metric in $(v, r)$ is
@eq-gr-eddington-finkelstein, and the outgoing slope $(1 + 2m/r)/(1 - 2m/r)$ in the $(r, v - r)$ plane is negative inside
$r = 2m$; (c) for a geodesic in the plane $\theta = \pi/2$ with conserved $E = (1 - 2m/r)\dot t$ and $L = r^2\dot\phi$, the radial
equation is $\ddot r = -\tfrac12V'(r)$ with
$$
V(r) = \Bigl(1 - \frac{2m}{r}\Bigr)\Bigl(1 + \frac{L^2}{r^2}\Bigr), \qquad \dot r^2 = E^2 - V(r),
$$ {#eq-gr-schwarzschild-potential}
circular orbits satisfy $mr^2 - L^2r + 3mL^2 = 0$, the innermost stable one is at $r = 6m$ with $L^2 = 12m^2$, and $u = 1/r$
obeys the orbit equation $u'' + u = m/L^2 + 3mu^2$; (d) numerically, the perihelion advances per revolution by
$6\pi m/p$, $p = L^2/m$, to within $3\%$ for $p = 300m$, $1000m$, $3000m$, and light passing at impact parameter $b$ is deflected
by $4m/b$ to within $5\%$ for $b = 200m$, $1000m$, $5000m$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Exact computation (`figures/schwarzschild.sage`), with SageManifolds for (a)-(c); (d) is
numerical.

r)$; outside the horizon (blue) the outgoing edge points to larger $r$, at $r = 2m$ it is vertical, and inside (red) both
edges point to smaller $r$. Centre: a bound geodesic with turning points $p/(1 \pm e)$, $p = 40m$, $e = 0.5$, over four

{{< interactive schwarzschild 460 >}}

The perihelion advance of Mercury was the first success of the theory. The example evaluates the formula of the
proposition with the orbit of Mercury.

::: {#exm-gr-mercury}
#### The perihelion of Mercury

Restoring units, the advance per orbit is $6\pi GM_\odot/(c^2a(1 - e^2))$ with $a = 5.79 \times 10^{10}\,$m and $e = 0.206$:
$5.0 \times 10^{-7}\,$rad. Mercury completes $415$ orbits per century, giving $2.1 \times 10^{-4}\,$rad $= 43''$ per
century, the anomaly that Newtonian perturbations by the other planets could not explain.
:::

The deflection of light by the Sun was measured during the eclipse of 1919. The formula of the proposition gives the
value for a ray grazing the solar surface.

::: {#exm-gr-light-bending}
#### Light bending by the Sun

For $b = R_\odot = 6.96 \times 10^8\,$m, $4GM_\odot/(c^2R_\odot) = 4 \times 1476\,\mathrm{m}/6.96 \times 10^8\,\mathrm{m} = 8.5 \times
10^{-6}\,$rad $= 1.75''$, twice the Newtonian value (@exr-gr-nl-light), as confirmed by the eclipse expedition and by
radio interferometry to better than $10^{-3}$.
:::

Close to the hole the orbits behave differently from Kepler's. Two radii mark the change, the innermost stable orbit
and the photon sphere.

::: {#exm-gr-isco}
#### The innermost stable orbit

Circular orbits exist down to $r = 3m$ and are stable only for $r \geq 6m$, where the two roots of $mr^2 - L^2r + 3mL^2 =
0$ merge. Matter in an accretion disc spirals in through stable orbits and plunges from $r = 6m$, having radiated the
fraction $1 - \sqrt{8/9} = 5.7\%$ of its rest energy (@exr-gr-isco-energy), far more than nuclear fusion releases.
:::

Kepler's third law survives in the Schwarzschild metric in a surprisingly exact form. The next example derives it and
the proper time of the orbiting body, which is not given by the same law.

::: {#exm-grb-kepler-exact}
#### Kepler's third law in Schwarzschild coordinates

For a circular geodesic $r = r_0$, $\ddot r = 0$ and the $r$-component of the geodesic equation reduces to $\Gamma^r_{tt}\dot t^2 + \Gamma^r_{\phi\phi}\dot\phi^2 = 0$,
that is $(m/r_0^2)(1 - 2m/r_0)\dot t^2 = r_0(1 - 2m/r_0)\dot\phi^2$. Hence $(d\phi/dt)^2 = m/r_0^3$ exactly, and the coordinate period is
$T = 2\pi\sqrt{r_0^3/GM}$, Kepler's law with no correction. The proper period is shorter: $d\tau^2 = (1 - 2m/r_0 - r_0^2\Omega^2)dt^2$ gives
$\tau = T\sqrt{1 - 3m/r_0}$, real only above the photon sphere $r_0 = 3m$ [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 2.72].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The photon sphere also sets the size of the black hole as seen from far away. The next example converts the critical
impact parameter of @exr-gr-photon-sphere into a cross-section.

::: {#exm-grb-capture}
#### The optical size of a black hole

Light from infinity with impact parameter $b < b_c = 3\sqrt3\,m$ is captured, and light with $b > b_c$ escapes. A black hole
therefore absorbs a beam over the area $\sigma = \pi b_c^2 = 27\pi G^2M^2/c^4$, and looks like a dark disc of radius $b_c \approx 2.6r_s$, larger
than its horizon by the lensing of rays that pass close to it. For the black hole M87* with $M = 6.5 \times 10^9M_\odot$ at $16.8\,$Mpc this
radius subtends about $20\,\mu$as, the scale of the shadow imaged in 2019 [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 2.76].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Light has its own effective potential, obtained from @eq-gr-schwarzschild-potential by dropping the rest mass. The
first exercise finds its maximum.

::: {#exr-gr-photon-sphere}
#### The photon sphere

For null geodesics $\dot r^2 = E^2 - (1 - 2m/r)L^2/r^2$. Find the radius of the unstable circular light orbit and the
critical impact parameter $b_c = L/E$ below which light is captured.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$W(r) = (1 - 2m/r)/r^2$ has $W' = 0$ at $r = 3m$, a maximum with $W(3m) = 1/(27m^2)$. A ray with $1/b^2 = E^2/L^2 >
1/(27m^2)$ passes over the barrier and falls in, so $b_c = 3\sqrt3\,m \approx 5.2m$; this is the size of the shadow of a black
hole as imaged by the Event Horizon Telescope.

{{< sage exr-gr-photon-sphere >}}
:::

The energy and angular momentum of circular orbits follow from @eq-gr-schwarzschild-potential. The second exercise
computes them and the binding energy at the innermost stable orbit.

::: {#exr-gr-isco-energy}
#### Energy of circular orbits

Show that a circular geodesic of radius $r > 3m$ has $L^2 = mr^2/(r - 3m)$ and $E^2 = (1 - 2m/r)^2/(1 - 3m/r)$, evaluate $E$
at $r = 6m$, and expand $E - 1$ at large $r$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$V'(r) = 0$ is linear in $L^2$ and gives $L^2 = mr^2/(r - 3m)$; then $E^2 = V(r)$ simplifies to $(1 - 2m/r)^2/(1 - 3m/r)$. At
$r = 6m$, $E = \sqrt{8/9} = 0.943$; at large $r$, $E - 1 \approx -m/(2r)$, the Newtonian energy of a circular orbit per unit
mass.

{{< sage exr-gr-isco-energy >}}
:::

The precession can also be found by perturbation theory instead of numerics. The third exercise derives the
coefficient $6\pi m/p$.

::: {#exr-gr-perihelion-perturbative}
#### The perihelion advance by perturbation theory

Write the orbit equation as $u'' + u = 1/p + 3mu^2$ with $p = L^2/m$ and treat $3mu^2$ as small. Show that $u = \tfrac1p(1 +
e\cos((1 - \epsilon)\phi))$ solves it to first order in $m/p$ and in $e$, with $\epsilon = 3m/p$, and deduce the advance $6\pi m/p$
per revolution.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Substituting, $u'' + u = \tfrac1p + \tfrac ep(1 - (1 - \epsilon)^2)\cos((1 - \epsilon)\phi) \approx \tfrac1p + \tfrac{2\epsilon e}{p}\cos(\dots)$, while
$3mu^2 \approx \tfrac{3m}{p^2}(1 + 2e\cos(\dots))$. The cosine terms match for $2\epsilon = 6m/p$, and the constant $3m/p^2$ only
shifts $p$ slightly. Perihelia ($u$ maximal) occur at $(1 - \epsilon)\phi = 2\pi k$, i.e. every $2\pi/(1 - \epsilon) \approx 2\pi(1 +
\epsilon)$: the advance per revolution is $2\pi\epsilon = 6\pi m/p$, the value checked numerically in @prp-gr-schwarzschild.
:::

Clocks on circular orbits run differently from clocks at rest at the same radius. The next exercise compares them for
an orbit like that of the GPS satellites, with Sage.

::: {#exr-grb-orbit-vs-static}
#### An orbiting clock and a static clock

At radius $r_0$ in the Schwarzschild metric ($G = c = 1$, $r_s = 2m$) a satellite moves on a circular geodesic and a static observer hovers.
With Sage: (a) write the satellite's four-velocity as $U = \alpha\partial_t + \beta\partial_\phi$ and find $\alpha$, $\beta$; (b) find their relative speed from
$\gamma = g(U, V)$; (c) find the ratio of the times that their clocks show between two meetings; (d) evaluate for $r_s = 8.87\,$mm and
$r_0 = 26\,560\,$km [@blennow2022relativity, Problems 2.99 and 2.100].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $\Omega = d\phi/dt = \sqrt{m/r_0^3}$ from @exm-grb-kepler-exact, $\alpha = (1 - 3r_s/2r_0)^{-1/2}$ and $\beta = \alpha\Omega$:

{{< sage exr-grb-orbit-vs-static >}}

The relative speed is $v = \sqrt{r_s/2(r_0 - r_s)}$, the Newtonian orbital speed corrected by the static observer's clock, and the
orbiting clock falls behind by the factor $1/\gamma$: $8 \times 10^{-11}$, about $7\,\mu$s per day, the special-relativistic part of the GPS
correction of @exr-gr-gps-clock.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A slightly perturbed circular orbit oscillates radially, and the oscillation is slower than the orbit. The next
exercise computes the ratio of the two periods, which is the perihelion advance in another form.

::: {#exr-grb-epicycles}
#### Radial oscillations about a circular orbit

For a geodesic close to the circular orbit $r = r_0$, write $r = r_0 + \rho$ and use @eq-gr-schwarzschild-potential to show with Sage that $\rho$ oscillates
with $\omega_r^2 = \tfrac12V''(r_0)$, and that the ratio of the radial period to the orbital period is $(1 - 6m/r_0)^{-1/2}$. Deduce the perihelion
advance per orbit for $r_0 \gg m$ [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 2.75].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Differentiating $\dot r^2 = E^2 - V$ gives $\ddot\rho = -\tfrac12V''(r_0)\rho$; both frequencies are taken in proper time, so their ratio is
independent of the time used:

{{< sage exr-grb-epicycles >}}

The radial period exceeds the orbital one, so the perihelion comes back after the angle $2\pi(1 - 6m/r_0)^{-1/2} \approx 2\pi + 6\pi m/r_0$,
the advance of @exm-gr-mercury for a circular orbit. At $r_0 = 6m$ the radial frequency vanishes: the innermost stable orbit.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

### Cosmology

On the largest scales the universe looks the same in every direction and, as far as we can tell, at every place.
The metrics with this symmetry have spatial sections of constant curvature, and all their time dependence sits in a
single scale factor.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-gr-flrw-metric}
#### FLRW metric

The **Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) metric** is
$$
ds^2 = dt^2 - a(t)^2\Bigl(\frac{dr^2}{1 - kr^2} + r^2d\theta^2 + r^2\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2\Bigr), \qquad k \in \{1, 0, -1\},
$$ {#eq-gr-flrw}
with **scale factor** $a(t) > 0$. Its spatial sections $t = \text{const}$ are maximally symmetric (@def-maximally-symmetric):
a three-sphere for $k = 1$, flat space for $k = 0$ and hyperbolic space for $k = -1$. The curves of constant $(r, \theta,
\phi)$ are the geodesics of **comoving** observers, whose proper time is $t$, and $H = \dot a/a$ is the **Hubble rate**
[@carroll1997, ch. 8, with the overall sign of our signature].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
De Sitter space in flat slicing is an FLRW metric. It is the simplest one with a non-constant scale factor.

::: {#exm-gr-flrw-de-sitter}
#### De Sitter space

$k = 0$ and $a = e^{Ht}$ give the metric of @exm-spacetime-de-sitter, with constant Hubble rate $H$
(@exm-gr-ds-hubble). Minkowski space is $k = 0$, $a = 1$.
:::

The scale factor converts comoving coordinate distances into physical distances. Its rate of change gives Hubble's
law, the linear relation between distance and recession speed.

::: {#exm-gr-flrw-hubble-law}
#### Hubble's law

Two comoving galaxies at coordinate separation $\Delta r$ (with $k = 0$) are at physical distance $d = a\,\Delta r$, so $\dot d
= Hd$. The measured value today, $H_0 \approx 70\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$, gives the Hubble time $1/H_0 \approx 14 \times
10^9$ years, the time scale of the expansion.
:::

The three values of $k$ are three different spatial geometries. The case $k = 1$ is a sphere in disguise.

::: {#exm-gr-flrw-closed}
#### The closed universe

For $k = 1$ put $r = \sin\chi$: then $dr^2/(1 - r^2) + r^2d\Omega^2 = d\chi^2 + \sin^2\chi\,d\Omega^2$, the round metric of the
unit three-sphere, and the universe has finite volume $2\pi^2a^3$. For $k = -1$, $r = \sinh\chi$ gives the hyperbolic metric
$d\chi^2 + \sinh^2\chi\,d\Omega^2$.
:::

An FLRW metric need not describe a curved spacetime. The next example is an expanding universe that is flat Minkowski
space in disguise, the Milne universe.

::: {#exm-grb-milne}
#### A universe that is flat spacetime

In $1 + 1$ dimensions let $a = Ht$. With $T = t\cosh(Hx)$, $X = t\sinh(Hx)$, $dT^2 - dX^2 = dt^2 - t^2H^2dx^2$: the metric is the interior of the future
light cone $T > |X|$ of Minkowski space, and the comoving observers are the straight lines through the origin, moving apart
at constant speeds. Light obeys $H\,dx = dt/t$, so $x = H^{-1}\ln(t/t_0)$ grows without bound and there is no horizon. The same
holds in $3 + 1$ dimensions for $k = -1$ and $a = t$ [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 2.137].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Light travelling through an expanding universe is stretched with it. The first exercise derives the cosmological
redshift from the null geodesics of the metric.

::: {#exr-gr-flrw-redshift}
#### The cosmological redshift

A radial light ray obeys $dt/a(t) = dr/\sqrt{1 - kr^2}$. Two wave crests emitted at $t_e$ and $t_e + \delta t_e$ by a comoving
source arrive at a comoving observer at $t_o$ and $t_o + \delta t_o$. Show that $\delta t_o/\delta t_e = a(t_o)/a(t_e)$, so that the
redshift is $1 + z = a(t_o)/a(t_e)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The comoving distance $\int dr/\sqrt{1 - kr^2}$ between source and observer is fixed, so $\int_{t_e}^{t_o}dt/a =
\int_{t_e + \delta t_e}^{t_o + \delta t_o}dt/a$, which for short intervals gives $\delta t_o/a(t_o) = \delta t_e/a(t_e)$. Frequencies scale
inversely: $\nu_o/\nu_e = a(t_e)/a(t_o)$, and wavelengths grow with the universe. This is the photon case of the $1/a$
law of @exr-gr-ds-peculiar.
:::

The spatial sections were claimed to have constant curvature. The second exercise checks this with SageManifolds for
all three values of $k$ at once.

::: {#exr-gr-flrw-spatial-curvature}
#### Constant spatial curvature

Compute the Ricci tensor and scalar curvature of the positive-definite metric $\gamma = dr^2/(1 - kr^2) + r^2d\Omega^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$R_{ij} = 2k\gamma_{ij}$ and $R = 6k$: the Einstein metric of a space of constant sectional curvature $k$, the three-sphere of
unit radius for $k = 1$ (@exm-einstein-spheres) and its flat and hyperbolic analogues.

{{< sage exr-gr-flrw-spatial-curvature >}}
:::

Changing the time coordinate can make an FLRW metric conformally flat. The third exercise does this for de Sitter
space.

::: {#exr-gr-flrw-conformal}
#### Conformal time

For $k = 0$ define the **conformal time** $\eta$ by $d\eta = dt/a$, so that $ds^2 = a(\eta)^2(d\eta^2 - d\vec x^2)$. For $a = e^{Ht}$
find $\eta(t)$ and $a(\eta)$, and verify that $(d\eta^2 - d\vec x^2)/(H\eta)^2$ has $R_{\mu\nu} = -3H^2g_{\mu\nu}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\eta = -e^{-Ht}/H$, which runs over $(-\infty, 0)$ as $t$ runs over $\mathbb{R}$, and $a = -1/(H\eta)$. The metric
$(H\eta)^{-2}(d\eta^2 - d\vec x^2)$ is conformal to Minkowski space and is again de Sitter space, with the curvature of
@exr-de-sitter-4d. Light rays are the lines $|d\vec x| = d\eta$, so the horizon of @exm-gr-ds-horizon is the finite range
of $\eta$.

{{< sage exr-gr-flrw-conformal >}}
:::

Light rays sent radially stay radial in an FLRW universe, which the redshift computations always assume. The next
exercise proves it from the geodesic equations.

::: {#exr-grb-radial-null}
#### Radial rays stay radial

Write the $\theta$ and $\phi$ components of the geodesic equation of @eq-gr-flrw and show that a geodesic with $\dot\theta = \dot\phi = 0$ at one point
has constant $\theta$ and $\phi$. Why does this not depend on where the origin $r = 0$ is put? [@plebanski2024introduction, Sec. 17.17,
Exercise 2]
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\ddot\theta + 2\tfrac{\dot a}{a}\dot t\dot\theta + \tfrac2r\dot r\dot\theta - \sin\theta\cos\theta\,\dot\phi^2 = 0$ and $\ddot\phi + 2\tfrac{\dot a}{a}\dot t\dot\phi + \tfrac2r\dot r\dot\phi + 2\cot\theta\,\dot\theta\dot\phi = 0$. Both
are satisfied by constant $\theta$, $\phi$ whatever $t(\sigma)$ and $r(\sigma)$ are, and the remaining $t$ and $r$ equations then have a solution for
the given initial data; by uniqueness of solutions of the geodesic equation it is the geodesic. Every point of an FLRW space is
equivalent to every other (the spatial sections are homogeneous), so the origin can be put at the emitter, and "radial" means
"through the origin" in any choice.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A closed one-dimensional universe lets a traveller go around it, if the expansion allows. The next exercise uses the
decay of peculiar momenta of @exr-gr-ds-peculiar to decide when.

::: {#exr-grb-circle-universe}
#### Around a circular universe

In $ds^2 = dt^2 - a(t)^2d\phi^2$ with $\phi \sim \phi + 2\pi$, an object leaves a comoving observer at $t_0$ with speed $v_0$ relative to it. Find its speed
$v(t)$ relative to the comoving observers and the condition for it to come back to the starting observer from the other side
[@blennow2022relativity, Problem 2.146].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$P = a^2\,d\phi/d\tau$ is conserved; the speed relative to comoving observers is $v = a\,d\phi/dt$ and $\gamma v = a\,d\phi/d\tau = P/a$, with $P =
a(t_0)\gamma_0v_0$. Hence $v(t) = P/\sqrt{a^2 + P^2}$, decreasing as $a$ grows. It completes the lap iff
$$
\int_{t_0}^\infty\frac{P\,dt}{a\sqrt{a^2 + P^2}} \geq 2\pi .
$$
For light ($P \to \infty$) the condition is $\int_{t_0}^\infty dt/a \geq 2\pi$; in de Sitter expansion $a = e^{Ht}$ the integral is finite, and a slow enough
universe (for example $a \propto t^{1/2}$) lets everything come back.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

The Einstein equations turn the scale factor into a dynamical variable. With a perfect fluid as source they become
two ordinary differential equations, the Friedmann equations.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-gr-friedmann-equations}
#### Friedmann equations

For the FLRW metric @eq-gr-flrw with a perfect fluid at rest (@exm-stress-fluid, $u = \partial_t$) of density $\rho(t)$ and
pressure $p(t)$, the **Friedmann equations** are
$$
H^2 = \Bigl(\frac{\dot a}{a}\Bigr)^2 = \frac{8\pi G}{3}\rho - \frac{k}{a^2}, \qquad \frac{\ddot a}{a} = -\frac{4\pi G}{3}(\rho + 3p),
$$ {#eq-gr-friedmann}
and they imply the **continuity equation** $\dot\rho + 3H(\rho + p) = 0$. For an equation of state $p = w\rho$ with
constant $w$ this gives $\rho \propto a^{-3(1 + w)}$. The **critical density** $\rho_c = 3H^2/(8\pi G)$ is the density of a
flat universe, and $\Omega = \rho/\rho_c$ is the **density parameter** [@carroll1997, ch. 8].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Ordinary matter at late times is pressureless dust, galaxies moving slowly relative to the comoving frame. Its
density dilutes with the volume.

::: {#exm-gr-friedmann-matter}
#### A matter-dominated universe

For dust, $w = 0$ and $\rho \propto a^{-3}$. With $k = 0$ the first equation is $\dot a^2 \propto 1/a$, solved by $a \propto t^{2/3}$:
the expansion decelerates, and the age of the universe is $t_0 = 2/(3H_0)$.
:::

In the early universe radiation dominates. Its energy density falls faster than that of matter because each photon is
also redshifted.

::: {#exm-gr-friedmann-radiation}
#### A radiation-dominated universe

For radiation, $w = \tfrac13$ (@exr-gr-fluid-trace) and $\rho \propto a^{-4}$: $a^{-3}$ from the volume and $a^{-1}$ from the
redshift of each photon (@exr-gr-flrw-redshift). With $k = 0$, $\dot a^2 \propto a^{-2}$ and $a \propto t^{1/2}$.
:::

A cosmological constant has $w = -1$, so its density does not dilute. The Friedmann equation then gives exponential
expansion, recovering de Sitter space.

::: {#exm-gr-friedmann-lambda}
#### A cosmological constant

With $\rho = \rho_\Lambda = \Lambda/(8\pi G)$ constant (@exr-gr-lambda-pressure) and $k = 0$, $H^2 = \Lambda/3$ is constant and $a =
e^{Ht}$: the vacuum solution of @exm-vacuum-de-sitter with $\Lambda = 3H^2$, now read as a cosmology. Since $\rho + 3p = -2\rho
< 0$, $\ddot a > 0$: the expansion accelerates.
:::

A cosmological constant drives the universe towards flatness. The next example quantifies this, the argument by which
inflation explains why the universe is so close to flat today.

::: {#exm-grb-inflation-flatness}
#### Inflation flattens the universe

The first Friedmann equation can be written $\Omega - 1 = k/\dot a^2$. During a phase dominated by a constant density, $a \propto e^{Ht}$ and
$\dot a = Ha$ grows exponentially, so $|\Omega - 1| \propto e^{-2Ht}$. After $N$ e-folds of expansion $|\Omega - 1|$ is reduced by $e^{-2N}$:
$N = 60$ gives $e^{-120} \approx 10^{-52}$, enough to make any initial curvature negligible, whereas during radiation or matter domination
$|\Omega - 1|$ grows like $t$ or $t^{2/3}$ [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 2.143].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The critical density sets the scale of cosmological densities. The first exercise evaluates it for the measured Hubble
rate and compares it with ordinary matter.

::: {#exr-gr-friedmann-critical-density}
#### The critical density

Evaluate $\rho_c = 3H_0^2/(8\pi G)$ for $H_0 = 70\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$ ($1\,\mathrm{Mpc} = 3.086 \times 10^{22}\,$m) in
$\mathrm{kg/m^3}$ and in hydrogen atoms per cubic metre ($m_H = 1.67 \times 10^{-27}\,$kg), and compare with the density of
@exr-gr-lambda-value.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$H_0 = 2.27 \times 10^{-18}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, so $\rho_c = 3(2.27 \times 10^{-18})^2/(8\pi \cdot 6.67 \times 10^{-11}) = 9.2 \times 10^{-27}\,
\mathrm{kg/m^3}$, about $5.5$ hydrogen atoms per cubic metre. The cosmological constant has $5.9 \times 10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$,
$\Omega_\Lambda \approx 0.64$ for this $H_0$: most of the energy of the universe is in the vacuum.
:::

The three examples are special cases of a single power law. The second exercise derives it for any $w > -1$.

::: {#exr-gr-friedmann-w}
#### A general equation of state

For $k = 0$ and $p = w\rho$ with $w > -1$, show that $a = t^{2/(3(1 + w))}$ solves both Friedmann equations with $\rho =
1/(6\pi G(1 + w)^2t^2)$, and that $\rho a^{3(1 + w)}$ is constant.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$H = \tfrac{2}{3(1 + w)t}$, so $H^2 = \tfrac{4}{9(1 + w)^2t^2} = \tfrac{8\pi G}{3}\rho$; the second equation follows similarly, and
$\rho a^{3(1 + w)} = 1/(6\pi G(1 + w)^2)$. The cases $w = 0$ and $w = \tfrac13$ are @exm-gr-friedmann-matter and
@exm-gr-friedmann-radiation; as $w \to -1$ the exponent diverges, the limit being the exponential of
@exm-gr-friedmann-lambda.

{{< sage exr-gr-friedmann-w >}}
:::

With positive curvature a matter-dominated universe recollapses. The third exercise solves the Friedmann equation in
that case in parametric form.

::: {#exr-gr-friedmann-closed}
#### The closed matter universe

For $k = 1$ and dust, the first Friedmann equation is $\dot a^2 + 1 = 2A/a$ with the constant $2A = \tfrac{8\pi G}{3}\rho a^3$.
Show that $a = A(1 - \cos\eta)$, $t = A(\eta - \sin\eta)$ solves it, and find the maximal size and the lifetime.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\dot a = \tfrac{da/d\eta}{dt/d\eta} = \tfrac{\sin\eta}{1 - \cos\eta}$, so $\dot a^2 + 1 = \tfrac{2}{1 - \cos\eta} = \tfrac{2A}{a}$: the curve
is a cycloid. The universe expands from $a = 0$ to $a_{\max} = 2A$ at $\eta = \pi$ and recollapses to a big crunch at $\eta = 2\pi$,
$t = 2\pi A$. Here $\eta$ is the conformal time of @exr-gr-flrw-conformal, since $dt/d\eta = a$.

{{< sage exr-gr-friedmann-closed >}}
:::

The previous example rests on the sign of $\ddot a$. The next exercise turns it into the condition on the equation of
state under which the curvature becomes less important with time.

::: {#exr-grb-flatness}
#### When the curvature fades

For an expanding FLRW universe with $p = w\rho$, show that $\Omega_k = -k/(aH)^2 = -k/\dot a^2$ decreases in magnitude iff $w < -\tfrac13$. Explain
the flatness problem in this language [@blennow2022relativity, Problems 2.143 and 2.148].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$|\Omega_k| = |k|/\dot a^2$ decreases iff $\dot a^2$ increases, iff $\ddot a > 0$ (with $\dot a > 0$), and by @eq-gr-friedmann iff $\rho + 3p = (1 + 3w)\rho < 0$, that is
$w < -\tfrac13$. Radiation ($w = \tfrac13$) and matter ($w = 0$) make $|\Omega_k|$ grow, so a universe with $|\Omega_k| \lesssim 0.01$ today had
$|\Omega_k| \lesssim 10^{-60}$ at the Planck time: an unexplained fine tuning unless a phase with $w < -\tfrac13$, inflation, came first.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

That the Friedmann equations follow from the Einstein equations is a computation with the curvature of
@eq-gr-flrw. SageManifolds performs it for arbitrary $a(t)$ and $k$; the proposition also records the exact solutions
plotted in @fig-flrw-scale-factor.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-gr-friedmann}
#### Friedmann equations from the Einstein equations

For @eq-gr-flrw the Einstein tensor is diagonal with $G_{tt} = 3(\dot a^2 + k)/a^2$ and $G_{ij} = -(2a\ddot a + \dot a^2 +
k)\gamma_{ij}$, where $g_{ij} = -a^2\gamma_{ij}$, and $R = -6(a\ddot a + \dot a^2 + k)/a^2$. With the perfect fluid at rest,
$G_{\mu\nu} = 8\pi GT_{\mu\nu}$ is equivalent to @eq-gr-friedmann, whose two equations imply the continuity equation. For
$k = 0$, $a \propto t^{2/3}$ ($p = 0$), $a \propto t^{1/2}$ ($p = \rho/3$) and $a \propto e^{Ht}$ ($p = -\rho$) are solutions, and with
matter and a cosmological constant, $\Omega_m + \Omega_\Lambda = 1$,
$$
a(t) = \Bigl(\frac{\Omega_m}{\Omega_\Lambda}\Bigr)^{1/3}\sinh^{2/3}\Bigl(\tfrac32\sqrt{\Omega_\Lambda}\,H_0t\Bigr)
$$ {#eq-gr-lcdm}
solves $H^2 = H_0^2(\Omega_ma^{-3} + \Omega_\Lambda)$; its age is $H_0t_0 = \tfrac{2}{3\sqrt{\Omega_\Lambda}}\operatorname{arcsinh}\sqrt{\Omega_\Lambda/
\Omega_m} = 0.964$ for $\Omega_m = 0.3$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Exact computation (`figures/flrw_scale_factor.sage`), with SageManifolds for the curvature.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
![The scale factor of a flat universe, normalised to $a(t_0) = 1$ and $\dot a(t_0) = H_0$ today, against $\tau = H_0(t -
t_0)$: radiation $a = (1 + 2\tau)^{1/2}$, matter $a = (1 + 3\tau/2)^{2/3}$, a cosmological constant $a = e^\tau$, and the mixture
$\Omega_m = 0.3$, $\Omega_\Lambda = 0.7$ of @eq-gr-lcdm, which starts like matter and ends like $\Lambda$. The big bang $a = 0$ is
at $\tau = -1/2$, $-2/3$ and $-0.964$; the de Sitter universe has none. The interactive version varies $\Omega_\Lambda$.
Generated by `figures/flrw_scale_factor.sage`.](figures/flrw_scale_factor.svg){#fig-flrw-scale-factor width=75%}

{{< interactive flrw_scale_factor 460 >}}

The age of the universe follows from @eq-gr-lcdm and the measured $H_0$. The first example compares it with the
matter-only value.

::: {#exm-gr-age}
#### The age of the universe

With $1/H_0 = 13.97 \times 10^9$ years ($H_0 = 70\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$), a matter-only flat universe would be $9.3$
billion years old, younger than the oldest stars; with $\Omega_\Lambda = 0.7$ the age is $0.964/H_0 = 13.5$ billion years
(@exr-gr-lcdm-age), one of the arguments for the cosmological constant.
:::

Whether the expansion speeds up or slows down is decided by the second Friedmann equation. Only a negative enough
pressure accelerates it.

::: {#exm-gr-acceleration}
#### Acceleration

$\ddot a > 0$ requires $\rho + 3p < 0$, i.e. $w < -\tfrac13$. Matter and radiation decelerate the expansion; the cosmological
constant accelerates it. For the mixture of @eq-gr-lcdm the deceleration parameter $q = -a\ddot a/\dot a^2$ is today
$q_0 = \tfrac12\Omega_m - \Omega_\Lambda = -0.55$ (@exr-gr-deceleration): the expansion is accelerating, as observed with distant
supernovae in 1998.
:::

The two components of @eq-gr-lcdm dominate at different times. Their densities are equal at a definite moment, and
acceleration starts somewhat earlier.

::: {#exm-gr-equality}
#### Matter-$\Lambda$ equality

$\rho_m \propto a^{-3}$ equals the constant $\rho_\Lambda$ at $a = (\Omega_m/\Omega_\Lambda)^{1/3} = 0.75$, redshift $z = 0.33$. The
acceleration $\ddot a > 0$ begins when $\rho_m = 2\rho_\Lambda$, at $a = (\Omega_m/2\Omega_\Lambda)^{1/3} = 0.60$, $z = 0.67$: this is the
inflection point of the black curve in @fig-flrw-scale-factor.
:::

Radiation dominated the early universe and matter took over later. The next example locates the change with today's
density parameters, as @exm-gr-equality did for matter and the cosmological constant.

::: {#exm-grb-radiation-equality}
#### Matter-radiation equality

$\rho_r \propto a^{-4}$ and $\rho_m \propto a^{-3}$ are equal at $a_{\mathrm{eq}} = \Omega_r/\Omega_m$. With $\Omega_m = 0.3$ and $\Omega_r = 10^{-4}$ this is $a_{\mathrm{eq}} =
3.3 \times 10^{-4}$, the redshift $z_{\mathrm{eq}} = \Omega_m/\Omega_r - 1 \approx 3000$. The cosmic microwave background was released at $z \approx 1100$,
after equality, in a matter-dominated universe; the temperature at equality was $T_0(1 + z_{\mathrm{eq}}) \approx 8000\,$K
[@blennow2022relativity, Problem 2.144].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The deceleration parameter summarises the second Friedmann equation in one number. The first exercise computes it for
a single fluid and for a mixture.

::: {#exr-gr-deceleration}
#### The deceleration parameter

Show that for $k = 0$ and a single fluid with $p = w\rho$, $q = -a\ddot a/\dot a^2 = \tfrac12(1 + 3w)$, and that for matter plus a
cosmological constant $q = \tfrac12\Omega_m - \Omega_\Lambda$ with the density parameters at the same time.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Dividing the second Friedmann equation by $H^2 = 8\pi G\rho/3$: $q = \tfrac{4\pi G(\rho + 3p)}{3H^2} = \tfrac12(1 + 3w)$; matter has
$q = \tfrac12$, radiation $q = 1$, $\Lambda$ $q = -1$. For a mixture the contributions add with weights $\Omega_i = \rho_i/\rho_c$:
$q = \sum_i\tfrac12(1 + 3w_i)\Omega_i = \tfrac12\Omega_m - \Omega_\Lambda$, which is $-0.55$ for $\Omega_m = 0.3$.
:::

The closed form of the age can be checked against direct numerical integration. The second exercise does both in
Sage.

::: {#exr-gr-lcdm-age}
#### The age by integration

Show that $t_0 = \int_0^1\frac{da}{aH(a)}$ and evaluate it numerically for $H = H_0\sqrt{\Omega_ma^{-3} + \Omega_\Lambda}$ with $\Omega_m = 0.
3$; compare with the closed form of @prp-gr-friedmann and convert to years.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$dt = da/\dot a = da/(aH)$. Both the integral and the closed form give $H_0t_0 = 0.9641$, i.e. $13.5$ billion years for
$1/H_0 = 13.97$ billion years, against $9.3$ for matter alone.

{{< sage exr-gr-lcdm-age >}}
:::

The early universe contained both radiation and matter. The third exercise solves the Friedmann equation exactly for
the mixture, using the conformal time of @exr-gr-flrw-conformal.

::: {#exr-gr-radiation-matter}
#### Radiation and matter

For $k = 0$ with radiation and dust, show that in conformal time the first Friedmann equation is $(da/d\eta)^2 = C_r +
C_ma$ with constants $C_r = \tfrac{8\pi G}{3}\rho_ra^4$, $C_m = \tfrac{8\pi G}{3}\rho_ma^3$, and that $a = \sqrt{C_r}\,\eta +
\tfrac14C_m\eta^2$ solves it. Recover the two power laws of the examples as limits, and find $\eta$ at equality $\rho_r = \rho_m$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\dot a = a^{-1}da/d\eta$, so $\dot a^2/a^2 = \tfrac{8\pi G}{3}(\rho_r + \rho_m)$ becomes $(da/d\eta)^2 = C_r + C_ma$, and the quadratic
solves it identically. With $t = \int a\,d\eta = \tfrac12\sqrt{C_r}\eta^2 + \tfrac1{12}C_m\eta^3$: for small $\eta$, $a \approx
(2\sqrt{C_r}\,t)^{1/2}$, radiation-like; for large $\eta$, $a \propto \eta^2 \propto t^{2/3}$, matter-like. Equality, $a = C_r/C_m$, is at
$\eta = 2(\sqrt2 - 1)\sqrt{C_r}/C_m$.

{{< sage exr-gr-radiation-matter >}}
:::

The time since equality follows from an integral that can be done in closed form. The next exercise evaluates it with
Sage for a flat universe of matter and radiation.

::: {#exr-grb-equality-time}
#### The time since equality

For a flat universe with $\Omega_r = x \ll 1$ and $\Omega_m = 1 - x$ today, compute $H_0t(a) = \int_0^a a'\,da'/\sqrt{x + (1 - x)a'}$ with Sage and the
time $t_0 - t_{\mathrm{eq}}$ elapsed since equality. Evaluate for $x = 10^{-3}$, $10^{-4}$ and $8.5 \times 10^{-5}$ [@blennow2022relativity, Problem 2.147].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$dt = da/(aH)$ with $H = H_0\sqrt{xa^{-4} + (1 - x)a^{-3}}$ gives the integrand; Sage finds the closed form and the numbers:

{{< sage exr-grb-equality-time >}}

The result is $\tfrac{2}{3H_0}$ up to corrections of order $x$: equality happened so early (about $3 \times 10^{-7}/H_0$, a few thousand years in this model)
that the elapsed time is the age of a pure matter universe.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The Friedmann equations used only the diagonal components of the Einstein tensor. The next exercise checks with Sage that
the others vanish, in two of the coordinate systems used for the FLRW metric.

::: {#exr-grb-rw-einstein}
#### The Einstein tensor of the FLRW metric

With Sage, compute the Einstein tensor of @eq-gr-flrw and of the $k = 1$ metric $dt^2 - a^2\bigl(d\chi^2 + \sin^2\chi\,d\Omega^2\bigr)$, show that it is diagonal in
both, and find $G_{tt}$ and $G^r{}_r$. Why must it be diagonal? [@plebanski2024introduction, Sec. 17.17, Exercise 1]
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
SageManifolds gives the components:

{{< sage exr-grb-rw-einstein >}}

$G_{tt} = 3(\dot a^2 + k)/a^2$ and $G^r{}_r = (\dot a^2 + 2a\ddot a + k)/a^2$ are the two Friedmann equations of @def-gr-friedmann-equations once $G_{\mu\nu} =
8\pi GT_{\mu\nu}$ is imposed with a perfect fluid at rest. The tensor must be diagonal because the spatial sections are isotropic: a
component $G_{ti}$ would be a preferred spatial vector, and $G_{ij} \propto g_{ij}$ is the only symmetric tensor invariant under rotations.
:::

## Exercises {#sec-general-relativity-exercises}

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The three exercises below combine the sections of the chapter. The first follows a test particle from the
symmetries of the Schwarzschild metric to Kepler's problem and its relativistic correction.

::: {#exr-gr-int-particle-orbits}
#### From symmetries to orbits

(a) Show that $\partial_t$ and $\partial_\phi$ are Killing vectors of @eq-gr-schwarzschild (@def-killing), and that $E =
g(\partial_t, u)$ and $L = -g(\partial_\phi, u)$ are conserved along geodesics. (b) Use $g(u, u) = 1$ to derive
@eq-gr-schwarzschild-potential. (c) Write $\tfrac12(V - 1)$ as the Newtonian effective potential of
@eq-effective-potential (per unit mass, $k = m$) plus a correction, and explain which term produces the perihelion advance
of @exr-gr-perihelion-perturbative.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) The metric components do not depend on $t$ or $\phi$, so $\mathcal{L}_{\partial_t}g = \mathcal{L}_{\partial_\phi}g = 0$; for a Killing
vector $\xi$ and a geodesic, $\tfrac{d}{d\tau}g(\xi, u) = \nabla_{(\mu}\xi_{\nu)}u^\mu u^\nu = 0$. Explicitly $E = (1 - 2m/r)\dot t$ and
$L = r^2\sin^2\theta\,\dot\phi$, and a rotation puts the orbit in the plane $\theta = \pi/2$. (b) $g(u, u) = (1 - 2m/r)\dot t^2 - (1 -
2m/r)^{-1}\dot r^2 - r^2\dot\phi^2 = 1$ becomes $E^2 - \dot r^2 = (1 - 2m/r)(1 + L^2/r^2)$ after multiplying by $1 - 2m/r$.
(c) $\tfrac12(V - 1) = -\tfrac mr + \tfrac{L^2}{2r^2} - \tfrac{mL^2}{r^3}$: Newton's $-k/r + L^2/2r^2$ plus an attractive $r^{-3}$ term.
It is the $r^{-3}$ term that becomes $3mu^2$ in the orbit equation and spoils the closure of the Kepler ellipses; the
energy equation $\tfrac12\dot r^2 + \tfrac12(V - 1) = \tfrac12(E^2 - 1)$ is otherwise Newton's, as in @exr-gr-nl-energy.

{{< sage exr-gr-int-particle-orbits >}}
:::

The second exercise looks at de Sitter space from the three points of view of the chapter. It appears as a maximally
symmetric vacuum, as a cosmology and as a static spacetime with a horizon.

::: {#exr-gr-int-de-sitter-three-ways}
#### De Sitter space three ways

(a) Show that the vacuum equations with $\Lambda > 0$ are solved by $ds^2 = dt^2 - e^{2Ht}d\vec x^2$ with $H^2 = \Lambda/3$
(@exr-de-sitter-4d). (b) Derive the same relation from the Friedmann equation with the density $\rho_\Lambda$ of
@exr-gr-lambda-pressure. (c) Show that the static metric $(1 - H^2r^2)dt^2 - (1 - H^2r^2)^{-1}dr^2 - r^2d\Omega^2$ also has $R_{\mu\nu} = -
3H^2g_{\mu\nu}$, and compare its horizon at $r = 1/H$ with that of @exm-gr-ds-horizon and with the Schwarzschild horizon.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) @exr-de-sitter-4d gives $R_{\mu\nu} = -3H^2g_{\mu\nu}$, i.e. $\Lambda = 3H^2$ by @exr-gr-vacuum-trace. (b) $\rho_\Lambda = \Lambda/(8\pi G)$ in
$H^2 = 8\pi G\rho/3$ gives $H^2 = \Lambda/3$ again (@exm-gr-friedmann-lambda). (c) SageManifolds gives $R_{\mu\nu} + 3H^2g_{\mu\nu} =
0$: it is the case $m = 0$ of @exr-gr-schwarzschild-de-sitter. Here $g_{tt}$ vanishes at $r = 1/H$, the physical distance
of @exm-gr-ds-horizon; unlike the Schwarzschild horizon it surrounds the observer, and every observer has their own.
The three metrics are coordinate patches of the same hyperboloid (@exm-gr-ds-hyperboloid).

{{< sage exr-gr-int-de-sitter-three-ways >}}
:::

The third exercise couples a scalar field to an expanding universe. It uses the stress tensor of
@sec-einstein-equations and the Friedmann equations of @sec-schwarzschild-flrw, and leads to the idea of inflation.

::: {#exr-gr-int-scalar-cosmology}
#### A scalar field in an expanding universe

Let $\phi(t)$ be a homogeneous scalar in flat FLRW. (a) From @exm-stress-scalar, show that it is a perfect fluid with $\rho =
\tfrac12\dot\phi^2 + V$ and $p = \tfrac12\dot\phi^2 - V$. (b) Show that $\Box\phi = \ddot\phi + 3H\dot\phi$ and that the continuity equation
of @def-gr-friedmann-equations is $\dot\phi$ times the field equation $\ddot\phi + 3H\dot\phi + V'(\phi) = 0$. (c) If $\dot\phi^2 \ll
V$, what is $w$, and how does $a(t)$ behave?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) With $\partial_i\phi = 0$, $T_{tt} = \dot\phi^2 - (\tfrac12\dot\phi^2 - V) = \tfrac12\dot\phi^2 + V$ and $T_{ij} = -g_{ij}(\tfrac12\dot\phi^2 - V)$,
which is $-pg_{ij}$ with $p = \tfrac12\dot\phi^2 - V$. (b) SageManifolds gives $\Box\phi = g^{\mu\nu}\nabla_\mu\nabla_\nu\phi = \ddot\phi +
3H\dot\phi$, the friction term coming from $\Gamma^i_{ti} = H$; and $\dot\rho + 3H(\rho + p) = \dot\phi(\ddot\phi + V'(\phi)) +
3H\dot\phi^2$, as stated (@exm-gr-variation-bianchi). (c) Then $p \approx -\rho$, $w \approx -1$, and the field acts as a slowly
varying cosmological constant: $H^2 \approx 8\pi GV/3$ and $a$ grows almost exponentially. This is **inflation**, the
accelerated expansion postulated for the very early universe.

{{< sage exr-gr-int-scalar-cosmology >}}
:::
::::
